label: Romans 1:2–4
text:
Paul's “prophets” here isn't limited to the major and minor prophets by name — it covers anyone through whom God spoke in advance, Moses and David included, since the promise of good news runs all through the Old Testament, not just the prophetic books. “Holy scriptures” drops the definite article in the Greek, throwing the weight onto quality rather than pointing at a specific known collection — these writings are holy by their very character, because they carry God's news.

“Was made” translates ginomai in an aorist participle, the verb of becoming rather than being — the same verb John uses for “the Word became flesh.” It marks entrance into a new condition: the eternal Son took on a human body and human limits, tracing his ancestry, “according to the flesh,” from David's line. “Declared” is a different verb, horizō, “to mark out the boundary, fix, appoint” — the root of our word “horizon.” It doesn't mean Jesus became Son of God at the resurrection; it means the resurrection is where that sonship, already and always true, was publicly marked out and put on display. Paul is careful with his preposition too — the Greek says only “of the dead” (nekrōn), not “out from among the dead,” tying Christ's rising to the resurrection of the dead as a category he inaugurates, not just his own solitary comeback.
translation: concerning his Son — who came to be, out of David's seed, according to the flesh; who was marked out as Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by resurrection of the dead.

label: Romans 1:5–7
text:
Paul's phrase “obedience of faith” is a genitive construction that cuts both ways in Greek — it can mean the obedience that consists in believing, or the obedience that faith itself produces once a person believes. Paul doesn't disambiguate; his commission from Christ is to bring the nations to whichever it is. “For his name's sake” uses the Old Testament idiom “the Name” — shorthand for the whole of who God has revealed himself to be, his reputation and character bundled into a single word, the way we'd say a man “has a name” for something. Paul's apostleship exists in honor of that whole revealed character.

“Called” (klētoi) is not a title someone earns or a label pinned on afterward — it's the effectual summons itself, the moment God's call reaches in and makes a person willing to receive it. Paul stacks two of these at the end: the Roman believers are “beloved of God” — plural, “God's loved-ones,” love in the sense of the cross — and “called saints,” which in the Greek is simply adjective plus noun, “called holy-ones.” It isn't that they were named and, separately, made holy; the calling itself is what constitutes them set-apart people, cut off from the ordinary and claimed for God.
translation: Through whom we received grace and a commission as apostle, to bring about among all the nations an obedience that flows from faith, for the sake of his Name — among whom you also are, called ones belonging to Jesus Christ — to all who are in Rome, God's loved-ones, called and thereby made holy ones. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

label: Romans 1:8
text: Paul's “first” here never gets a “second” — the thought runs on without the orderly list he seems to promise, which is just how the man's mind worked when he was excited. “Spoken of” translates kataggellō, a compound that means more than “reported” — it's to broadcast something down the line, hearer to hearer, with an implied note of commendation built in. The world wasn't just hearing gossip about the Roman church; it was hearing them praised. And planting a healthy, visibly faithful church in the capital of the empire — a city famous even among pagan writers for its appetite for vice — was itself a kind of proof that this new faith came from somewhere beyond Rome's own resources.
translation: First, I am continually giving thanks to my God through Jesus Christ concerning all of you, because your faith is being proclaimed abroad — with praise attached — in the whole world.

label: Romans 1:9–12
text:
“Witness” is martus, the word behind our “martyr” — someone testifying to what he's personally seen or known, even when it costs him. Paul calls on that kind of testimony because his prayer life for these strangers in Rome is invisible to everyone but God. “Serve” is latreuō, priestly language, the word used for the temple ministers' sacred duties — but Paul locates his priesthood “in my spirit,” his own inner life, not in an outward ritual performed at an altar. “Without ceasing” is built from a root meaning “to leave off” with a flat negative stuck on the front — not occasional prayer but prayer with no gaps in it.

“Prosperous journey” renders euodoō, a verb that originally pictured a short, easy road but had broadened by Paul's day to mean simply “to be granted success” in any venture. He piles up qualifiers — if somehow, now, at last — to show just how long he's been wanting this trip and how uncertain he still is that it will happen. And when he explains why, he catches himself mid-sentence: he'd meant to say he wanted to give them a “spiritual gift,” a charisma, but he softens it into something mutual — the verb is sumparakaleō, “to strengthen together with,” not one expert handing down help to novices but two parties leaning on each other's faith.
translation: For God is my witness, whom I am continually serving in my own spirit in the good news concerning his Son, how without ceasing I keep making mention of you, always asking in my prayers whether somehow, now at last, I might be granted a way to come to you — for I long to see you, so that I may impart to you some gift of the Spirit for your establishing, that is, that we may be strengthened together, each of us by the other's faith, yours and mine alike.

label: Romans 1:13
text: “Purposed” is protithēmi, literally “to set a thing out in front of yourself” — a deliberate plan, not a passing wish. The old “let” in “was let” is archaic English for “hindered”; the Greek verb, kōluō, means to cut something short before it can happen. And “have,” as in “have some fruit,” is an ingressive aorist — it isn't a state Paul wants to sit in but a result he wants to reach: not “keep having fruit” but “come to obtain it,” a onetime crossing of the finish line.
translation: I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that many times I planned to come to you — and was cut short until now — so that I might obtain some fruit among you too, just as among the rest of the nations.

label: Romans 1:14–15
text: “Debtor” is opheiletēs, a word for personal moral obligation — Paul owes the world his gospel not because circumstances force it on him but because grace laid a debt on him that only preaching can pay off. “Barbarian,” barbaros, began as pure sound-mimicry — the babbling “bar-bar” the Greeks heard when foreigners spoke — and hardened into the word for anyone outside Greek language and culture. And the pair “wise” and “unwise” carried a moral edge in Greek that's gone from the English: sophos wasn't mere cleverness but wisdom tied to goodness, while anoētos described a lack of understanding rooted in a moral failure, not simple ignorance. Paul's debt runs to every kind of person on both sides of every line the ancient world drew.
translation: Both to Greeks and to those who only babble, both to the wise and to those wanting in wisdom, I stand as a debtor. So, as far as it depends on me, I am eager to preach the good news to you also, who are in Rome.

label: Romans 1:16–17
text:
Paul had six different Greek words for “power” to choose from, and he reaches for dunamis — inherent, exerted power, the capacity built into a thing to do what it does. It isn't a loanword for explosives (the Greeks had no gunpowder to name); it's the ordinary word for operative strength. There's no definite article in front of it either — Paul isn't calling the gospel “the power of God” as if there were only one, but “a power of God,” a force at work in its own right, not merely a message about one.

“Righteousness of God” turns on a word, dikaiosunē, whose whole shape in Scripture differs from the Greek moral vocabulary around it — righteousness there is a social virtue measured against other people; righteousness here is conformity to God's own character, a status he defines and bestows, not one society negotiates. “Revealed” is apokaluptō, “to uncover,” the same root behind “apocalypse” — something previously hidden is pulled into the light. And the phrase “from faith to faith” traces a single line from source to destination: the righteousness comes by way of faith, its origin, and lands on faith, the only way to receive it — excluding, at both ends, any road through human merit.
translation: For I am not ashamed of the good news; it is a power of God, resulting in salvation for everyone who keeps believing — to the Jew first, and also to the Greek. For in it a righteousness of God is being uncovered, out of faith, into faith — just as it stands written: the one who is righteous by faith shall keep on living.

label: Romans 1:18
text: “Wrath,” orgē, isn't a flash of temper in the Greek any more than in the Hebrew behind it — it's the settled, principled opposition of a good being to evil, the necessary flip side of loving what's right. A being incapable of orgē would be a being indifferent to good and evil alike. “Ungodliness” (asebeia) names the vertical failure — irreverence toward God — while “hold down” (katechō) is active, not passive: this isn't people innocently lacking truth, it's people pressing a truth they do have back under the surface so it won't rise up and demand anything of them. The “truth” in view isn't the gospel — plenty of these people never heard it — it's the plain evidence of God visible in the created world, which people actively suppress rather than simply miss.
translation: For God's wrath is being uncovered from heaven against every irreverence and unrighteousness of men who are holding the truth down in unrighteousness.

label: Romans 1:19–20
text:
“The known thing” (to gnōston) is Paul's phrase, not “the knowable” — this is knowledge people actually possess, not merely knowledge available to them in theory. God did the showing himself (phaneroō, “made it visible”), and the paradox Paul builds is deliberate: the invisible things of God are “clearly seen” — reasoned out backward from the visible creation to the unseen cause behind it, the way anyone infers a builder from a building.

For “Godhead,” Paul reaches for theiotēs rather than theotēs, the word he uses elsewhere for Christ's full deity. Theiotēs is the broader, vaguer term — not “God-ness” itself but the sum of God's visible attributes, his power and majesty as they can be read off the natural world. That distinction matters: nature shows enough of God to leave everyone without excuse, but it doesn't show God himself the way his own Son does. “Without excuse,” anapologētos, is a courtroom word — literally “without a defense speech” — describing someone who has no argument left to make once the evidence is in.
translation: Because that which is known about God is plainly evident among them, for God himself made it visible to them. For his invisible qualities — his eternal power and his divine nature — have been, ever since the creation of the world, clearly seen, being perceived through the things that have been made — so that they are left without a defense.

label: Romans 1:21–23
text:
“Became vain” doesn't mean what English “vain” now suggests — not proud, but empty of result. Mataiōō is built on mataios, “futile,” the word for an effort that comes to nothing; Paul is describing minds that thought hard and arrived at nothing worth reaching. “Professing” (phaskō) marks unsupported assertion — claiming something as fact with nothing behind the claim — and it's paired with sophos, “wise” in the fullest classical sense: the Greek ideal of mental excellence, skill, and cultivation. The people Paul describes claimed that highest kind of wisdom for themselves.

What they got instead is named with a different word, mōrainō, built from the same root as our “moron” — not moral folly first, but plain stupefaction, a mind gone dull and insipid. And the exchange Paul traces runs on a straight verb, allassō, “to swap one thing for another”: the uncorruptible God traded for eikōn, a derived, secondhand likeness of corruptible man — and then, worse, of birds, four-footed animals, and things that crawl. The list runs downhill on purpose. As worship degrades, so does its object, a straight line from the incorruptible Creator down to a carved snake.
translation: Because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, nor did they give thanks, but they became futile in their reasonings, and their undiscerning heart was darkened. While claiming to be wise, they turned into fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for a likeness — an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed animals, and of creeping things.

label: Romans 1:24
text: “Gave up” is paradidōmi, a handing-over into someone else's control — the same verb used of handing a prisoner over to a jailer. This is judicial, not merely permissive: having chosen the creature over the Creator, humanity was handed over to the very cravings it had preferred. And Paul's preposition matters — the impurity happens “in” their hearts, a locative, meaning the desires themselves are the arena where the dishonoring takes place, not merely the tool used to bring it about.
translation: Because of this, God handed them over, within the passionate cravings of their own hearts, to impurity — the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves.

label: Romans 1:25
text: “More than the Creator” undersells the Greek preposition, para — it doesn't mean the creature simply outranked the Creator in their affections, it means the Creator was passed by altogether, bypassed rather than merely demoted. “Worshipped and served” pairs two acts: sebazomai, religious honor, and latreuō, the same cultic-service word Paul used earlier of his own ministry to God — now aimed, tragically, at the created thing instead of at him. “Blessed,” closing the sentence, is eulogētos, built from eu (“well”) and legō (“to speak”) — the source of our word “eulogy” — a doxology Paul can't help dropping in as soon as he's named God as Creator, even mid-indictment.
translation: They exchanged the truth of God for the lie, and gave religious honor and cultic service to the created thing rather than the Creator, who is to be well-spoken-of forever. Amen.

label: Romans 1:26
text: “Passions” (pathē) here is a narrower, harder word than the “lusts” (epithumia) of verse 24 — epithumia names the active craving, pathē the underlying diseased condition that produces it, a difference between a symptom and the sickness itself. “Vile,” atimia, is built straight from timē, “honor” or “proper valuation” — with the negating alpha in front, it means a wrong estimate of worth, treating something as less than what it actually is. And Paul's word for “women” here isn't the ordinary gunē but thēlus, “female” — the word that marks the biological distinction of sex rather than womanhood as such, because it's exactly that created distinction, phusis, “nature,” that is being set aside for its opposite, para phusin, “against nature.”
translation: Because of this, God handed them over to dishonoring passions. Even their females exchanged the natural use for what is against nature.

label: Romans 1:27
text: “Burned” (ekkaiō) has the intensifying ek- prefix built in — not simply “inflamed” but “burned out,” consumed to the end. Paul switches his word for “lust” too: not the usual epithumia but orexis, a rarer and stronger word for raw appetite. “Working” translates katergazomai, “to work a thing out to its finish” — this wasn't an isolated act but something carried through to completion. And “was meet,” edei, doesn't describe an externally imposed punishment; it names a necessity built into the nature of the case itself — the consequence wasn't handed down afterward, it was baked into the deviation (planē, “a wandering off course”) from the start.
translation: And likewise also the males, having left behind the natural use of the female, were burned out in their appetite toward one another — males working out with males what is shameful, and receiving back in themselves the payback that was, in the nature of the case, necessary for their wandering off course.

label: Romans 1:28
text: “Did not like to retain God” hides a courtroom image in English translation. Dokimazō means “to put on trial for the purpose of approving” — humanity tested God against its own specifications and, on that self-appointed jury, disapproved him. Paul's payback is a wordplay: since they rendered God adokimos — failed, disapproved — God in turn handed them over to a nous adokimos, a “disapproved mind,” a mind that itself fails the test a mind is supposed to pass. It's not merely wrong thinking; it's a mind no longer capable of functioning as a mind, its built-in sense of right and wrong short-circuited.
translation: And just as they, having tested God and found him not to their specifications, disapproved of holding him in full knowledge, God handed them over to a mind that fails the test — to do the things that are not fitting.

label: Romans 1:29–32
text: “Being filled” is a perfect participle — a completed action whose result has settled into a fixed state. This isn't a momentary lapse Paul is cataloguing; it's a condition people have arrived at and now simply live inside of. Twenty-one separate sins pile up in the list, among them astorgos, “without natural affection” — a compound that names the specific bond of love between parents and children, husbands and wives, now missing entirely. And Paul saves his sharpest observation for last: it's one thing to do these things, another, worse thing to applaud someone else doing them — approval of sin in another is a step further down than the sin itself, because it makes common cause with it on purpose, with a clear conscience.
translation: Filled with all unrighteousness — wickedness, greed, malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malignity — whisperers, slanderers, haters of God, insolent, arrogant, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, without understanding, faithless, without natural affection, unmerciful — who, though they know full well God's just decree that people who practice such things deserve death, not only keep doing them but applaud those who practice them.

label: Romans 2:1
text: “Inexcusable” repeats the exact word from 1:20 — anapologētos, “without a defense speech” — Paul is deliberately tying the moralizing critic back to the pagan he's just finished condemning: same word, same verdict. “Judgest” (krinō) here means censorious appraisal, sizing someone up unfavorably, while “condemn” stacks the preposition kata, “down,” onto that same root — to “judge down,” pass sentence. The critic's own sentence on someone else becomes, by the shared principle, a sentence on himself, since he's sinning against the very light by which he judges.
translation: Therefore you are without a defense, O man, every one of you who judges — for in that in which you judge the other, you condemn yourself, since you, the judge, keep on practicing the very same things.

label: Romans 2:2
text: “Know” here is oida, the verb for settled, given knowledge rather than knowledge gained by experience — Paul isn't arguing a case, he's stating something both he and his readers already take as certain: God's verdict lines up exactly with the facts, with no gap between what happened and what he rules.
translation: But we know with certainty that God's judgment is in accordance with truth against those who practice such things.

label: Romans 2:3
text: “Thinkest” is logizomai, a verb of calculation — Paul pictures the critic actually running the numbers and arriving at the conclusion that he personally will be exempt. And the Greek makes the pronoun emphatic: su, “you” — of all people, you, who can see clearly enough to judge someone else's sin, imagine you'll dodge the very judgment you're so quick to hand down.
translation: And do you, of all people — you who judge those who practice such things while doing the same yourself — do you reckon that you will escape the judgment of God?

label: Romans 2:4
text: “Despisest” is built the same way as our “look down on” — kataphroneō, phroneō (“to direct the mind toward”) plus kata (“down”). “Forbearance,” anochē, is a word borrowed from the language of a military truce — a temporary holding-back of hostilities, not a permanent amnesty, which is exactly Paul's point: God's patience has a term to it, not an open-ended one. And “leads to repentance” is present tense — God's kindness is actively, continuously doing this pulling toward repentance the whole time it's being ignored, not just once, at the start.
translation: Or are you treating with contempt the riches of his kindness and truce-like restraint and patience — not realizing that God's kindness is continually leading you toward repentance?

label: Romans 2:5
text: “Treasurest” is thēsaurizo, “to store something up” — the root behind our word “thesaurus,” a storehouse of words the way this is a storehouse of wrath. Every act of unrepentance makes another deposit. And “hardness” is sklērotēs, the word behind “sclerosis” — a stiffening, an obstinate rigidity that won't bend or break under the very kindness meant to soften it.
translation: But according to your hardened and unrepentant heart, you are storing up for yourself wrath — for the day of wrath, when God's righteous judgment will be uncovered.

label: Romans 2:6–10
text: “Render” is apodidōmi, reimbursement language — paying back exactly what's owed, not dispensing an arbitrary reward. “Patient continuance” is hupomonē, built on the idea of remaining under a weight rather than shrugging it off — willingly staying under discipline that the will would naturally resist. And on the other side, “anguish,” stenochōria, is literally “narrowness of place” — the word used for the crush of a besieged city, hemmed in with no room to move, set against the Psalms' opposite image of God bringing a person out “into a broad place.” The vocabulary itself pictures judgment as confinement and reward as spaciousness.
translation: He will pay back to each one according to his deeds — to those who by patiently remaining under a good work keep seeking glory, honor, and incorruption, eternal life; but to those who are factious and refuse persuasion by the truth while yielding to unrighteousness, wrath and anger. Pressure and confinement on every soul of man who works out evil to the end, the Jew first and also the Greek; but glory, honor, and peace to everyone who works out good to the end, the Jew first and also the Greek.

label: Romans 2:11–12
text: “Respect of persons” translates a single compound Greek word built from “face” and “receive” — literally “face-receiving,” the practice of favoring someone because of how they look or what standing they hold, rather than judging what's actually true of them. God, Paul says, does no such face-receiving. And the parallel he draws is exact: those without the law who sin will perish without reference to the law; those under the law who sin will be judged by the very law they had. Having the law changes the standard of judgment, not the fact of it.
translation: For there is no receiving of faces with God. For as many as sinned without law will also perish without law; and as many as sinned within the sphere of law will be judged by that law.

label: Romans 2:13
text: “Hearers” is akroatēs, not the ordinary word for someone who simply hears — it describes a student, someone whose regular business is sitting under instruction, week after week in the synagogue. Paul's point bites harder for the specificity: it isn't casual listeners he's talking about but people formally, faithfully trained in the law, and even their training doesn't count for anything without action attached to it.
translation: For it is not the ones who regularly sit under the law's instruction who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified.

label: Romans 2:14–16
text: “When,” hotan, sets up a general, recurring hypothetical — Paul isn't naming specific Gentiles but describing a pattern that shows up whenever it does. And “written on their hearts” plays off the old contrast with the law written on stone tables at Sinai — this is unwritten law, a moral sense built into people rather than handed to them on a document. Paul pictures a small courtroom running inside every person: their conduct testifies, their conscience corroborates the testimony, and their own thoughts take turns as prosecution and defense — apologeomai, literally “speaking in one's own defense” — arguing the case back and forth in a person's own head, with no outside law required to generate the argument.
translation: For whenever Gentiles, who have no law, do by nature the things the law requires, these, having no law, are a law to themselves — since they demonstrate the work of the law written on their hearts, their conscience bearing joint witness, and their own thoughts alternately accusing or even defending one another — on the day when God judges the hidden things of men, according to my gospel, through Jesus Christ.

label: Romans 2:17–20
text:
“Restest on the law” pictures leaning back on something for support — anapauō, the same verb used for resting one's whole weight on a couch. “Approvest the things that are excellent” is really “test with precision the things that differ” — dokimazō ta diapheronta, fine casuistic discrimination, the skill of drawing careful distinctions, trained by katēcheō, formal instruction — the word that gives us “catechism,” systematic, repeated teaching rather than a one-time lesson.

“Confident” sits in the perfect tense — a settled conviction reached once and never revisited, a closed case in the Jew's own mind. “Guide” is hodēgos, built from “road” and “lead,” while “instructor” is paideutēs, the word for the household slave whose job was walking a child to school and disciplining him along the way — closer to “corrector” than “teacher.” And “babes,” nēpion, literally “the non-speaking one,” was used both of infants and of raw converts still learning to talk the faith. Paul's last jab is “form” — morphōsis, not the full substance of a thing but its outline, a rough sketch of knowledge and truth rather than the finished portrait.
translation: Granted that you bear the name Jew, and lean your whole weight on the law, and boast in God, and know his will by experience, and — trained by regular catechetical instruction in the law — test with precision the things that differ and approve them; and have persuaded yourself, with a settled conviction, that you are a guide of the blind, a light to those in darkness, a corrector of the senseless, a teacher of infants, holding in the law the rough outline of knowledge and of the truth.

label: Romans 2:21–24
text: “Abhorrest” (bdelussō) began as a word for physical revulsion — literally to turn away from something because of its stench — before it settled into moral loathing. “Transgressing,” parabasis, is built from “step” plus “alongside/beyond” — stepping over a line that was clearly drawn, not stumbling in the dark but crossing a marked boundary on purpose. And Paul's rapid-fire questions — do you steal, while preaching against stealing; commit adultery, while forbidding it; rob temples, while recoiling from idols like they stink — build to the real charge: it's the transgressor's own conduct, not pagan hostility, that gets God's name spoken with contempt among the very nations he was supposed to be teaching.
translation: You, then, who teach another — do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say a person must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who turn from idols as from a stench — do you rob temples? You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by overstepping that same law? For, just as it stands written, the name of God is being blasphemed among the nations because of you.

label: Romans 2:25
text: “Is made” is gegonen, a perfect tense — not a temporary demotion but a settled, standing condition: once the law is broken, the circumcision that once meant something has become, and stays, uncircumcision in God's reckoning. “Keep” is prassō, habitual practice, ongoing conduct, not a single lapse — Paul's whole argument runs on the difference between a badge and a life actually lived out.
translation: For circumcision is indeed of value, if you are one who habitually practices the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become — and remains — uncircumcision.

label: Romans 2:26
text: “Counted” is logizomai, accounting language — crediting something to a ledger. And “keep” here is a different verb than in verse 25 — phulassō, “to guard,” picturing someone standing watch over the law's requirements so they don't get broken, in the present tense of habitual practice. The uncircumcised person who guards the law this way gets that guarding entered to his account as if it were circumcision itself.
translation: So if the uncircumcised man is habitually guarding the righteous requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be credited to him as circumcision?

label: Romans 2:27
text: “By nature” modifies “fulfilling the law” — the point being that this Gentile keeps the law's substance without any of the outward apparatus the Jew has: no written code, no bodily sign. “By” translates dia in the sense of “with the advantage of” — the Jew who transgresses does so in spite of every outward help stacked in his favor, which makes his failure, not his heritage, the thing that actually counts against him.
translation: And the physically uncircumcised man who, by nature, keeps on fulfilling the law, will judge you — you who, with the letter and circumcision as your advantage, are a transgressor of the law.

label: Romans 2:28–29
text: “Outwardly” and “inwardly” translate phaneros (“visible, apparent”) and kruptos (“hidden, secret”) — the whole passage turns on relocating the real identity markers from what can be seen to what can't. “In spirit” and “in letter” are both locative — they name a sphere of operation, not a method: true circumcision happens in the territory of a person's inner, God-conscious life, not in the territory of external rule-keeping. There may be a quiet wordplay buried here too — “Jew” descends from “Judah,” which means “praise” — so that the true Jew is, almost by definition, the one whose praise comes from God rather than from the applause of other people.
translation: For the one who is a Jew merely in outward appearance is not the true Jew, nor is circumcision merely in outward, fleshly form the true circumcision. But the one who is a Jew inwardly is the true Jew, and circumcision is of the heart, in the sphere of the spirit, not the letter — a circumcision whose praise comes not from men, but from God.

label: Romans 3:1
text: “Advantage” is perisson, “surplus” — something extra, over and above the baseline. Having just argued that circumcision counts for nothing without obedience, Paul anticipates the obvious objection forming in a Jewish reader's mind and states it as bluntly as possible before answering it: if none of that matters, what was the surplus for?
translation: What, then, is the surplus advantage of the Jew? Or what is the profit of circumcision?

label: Romans 3:2
text: "Chiefly" translates *prōton*, "first" -- Paul is opening a list he never finishes; he names one advantage of being a Jew and moves straight on. "Oracles" is *logia*, a term reserved for divine utterances, not writings in general. Israel's advantage was custodial, not moral: they were handed the actual words of God to keep safe, and at the time Paul wrote, that meant the Old Testament.
translation: Much, in every way -- for first of all, they were entrusted with the oracles of God.

label: Romans 3:5–8
text: "Commend" is *sunistēmi*, "to set together" -- proof-language. Paul's point is that human unrighteousness, set side by side with God's righteousness, throws the latter into sharper relief; the contrast demonstrates it rather than excusing the sin that supplies the contrast. "Taketh vengeance" is literally "brings the anger to bear" (*epipherō orgēn*) -- a controlled, judicial wrath, not a fit of temper. Paul flags his own courtroom analogy as borrowed speech ("I speak as a man"), aware that framing God's justice in human legal terms domesticates something too large for the comparison. And the slander in verse 8 -- "let us do evil that good may come" -- isn't a hypothetical Paul invents to knock down; it's the actual charge of lawlessness already being circulated against his gospel of grace.
translation: But if our unrighteousness demonstrates God's righteousness, what shall we say? God is not unrighteous to inflict wrath, is he? -- I speak in merely human terms. Let it not happen! Otherwise how will God judge the world? And if, as is the case, God's truth abounded to his glory by my falsehood, why am I still being judged as a sinner? And why not say -- as some report, slandering us, that we say -- Let us do evil so that good may come? Their condemnation is just.

label: Romans 3:9
text: "Are better" translates *proechō*, "to hold a place ahead of" -- a question of relative advantage, not moral superiority. "Proved" is a courtroom word (*proaitiaomai*, "to bring a charge beforehand"), not a term for logical demonstration. Paul isn't building a syllogism here so much as reading out an indictment already filed: his whole preceding argument has been a charge laid jointly against Jew and Gentile.
translation: What then? Are we ahead? Not at all -- for we have already brought the charge that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin.

label: Romans 3:10–12
text: "It is written" is a perfect tense (*gegraptai*) -- not "was written" but "stands written, and stands written still," a permanent record rather than a past event. "Seeketh after" (*ekzēteō*) describes an active, determined search, not idle curiosity -- and the text's claim is that no one is conducting it. "Gone out of the way" is literally "leaned out" (*ekklinō*, "lean" plus "out"), a gradual drift off the road rather than one dramatic wrong turn. And "become unprofitable" carries, in its underlying Hebrew sense, the picture of milk gone sour -- something that started good and curdled.
translation: As it stands written: There is no righteous person, not even one. There is no one who understands; no one who is searching out God. All have leaned off the road; together they have gone sour. There is no one continually doing good -- not so much as one.

label: Romans 3:13–18
text: The catalog of sins reads like a scan down the body, each organ implicated through its own ordinary function turned toward evil: throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet. "Their throat is an opened grave" uses a perfect participle -- the grave has been opened and stands open, reeking. "They have used deceit" is imperfect tense: not a single lie but people continuously smoothing their tongues into deception, habit rather than incident. The poison under the lips belongs specifically to the asp, the Egyptian cobra whose venom sac sits exactly there -- a precise image, not a stock metaphor for snakes in general. The list closes on the root rather than another symptom: "there is no fear of God before their eyes" is the cause everything before it is an effect of.
translation: Their throat is a grave standing open. With their tongues they kept on practicing deceit. The poison of asps is under their lips, whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness, whose feet run swiftly to pour out blood. Ruin and misery mark their roads, and the road of peace they have not known. There is no fear of God set before their eyes.

label: Romans 3:21–23
text: "Now" here marks a logical turn in the argument, not a moment in time. "Is manifested" is a perfect tense: God's righteousness has been disclosed and stands permanently on view, with the law and the prophets continually bearing it witness in the present. "Have sinned" is a constative aorist, a single wide-angle snapshot of the whole human race as one completed fact -- all sinned. But "come short" shifts to the present tense: not only a past verdict but an ongoing state, like a runner still trailing in a race that hasn't finished. That's the picture behind the verb itself, which properly means falling behind toward a finish line, not simply missing a target once.
translation: But now, apart from law, God's righteousness stands revealed, the law and the prophets continually bearing it witness -- God's righteousness through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe. For there is no distinction: all sinned, and all are still falling short of the glory of God.

label: Romans 3:24–26
text: Three different Greek verbs get rendered "redeem" across the New Testament, and the noun behind "redemption" here draws on the fullest of them -- paying a ransom price to set someone permanently free, not merely bidding for them in the slave market but taking them off it for good. "Set forth" (*protithēmi*) means displayed publicly, in the open -- a deliberate contrast with the mercy seat in the tabernacle, which sat behind a veil and was approached by one priest, once a year. Christ, by contrast, is put on exhibit for everyone to see. "Propitiation" is in fact the technical term (*hilastērion*) for that very mercy seat, the golden cover over the ark where the sacrificial blood was sprinkled -- not language for buying off an angry god, but for the object where blood turns a place of judgment into a place of mercy. And "remission" translates a rare word found nowhere else in the New Testament that means "passing over" rather than "putting away": God didn't excuse sins committed before the cross, he held them in abeyance, forbearing to punish because the reckoning that would settle the account was still ahead.
translation: Having been declared righteous freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus -- whom God publicly displayed as a mercy seat, through faith in his blood, to demonstrate his righteousness, on account of his passing over sins previously committed, in the forbearance of God -- to demonstrate his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be both righteous, and the one who declares righteous the one who has faith in Jesus.

label: Romans 3:29–31
text: Paul switches prepositions mid-sentence for "faith" -- *ek pisteōs*, "out of faith" as a source, then *dia pisteōs*, "through faith" as a means -- almost certainly for rhetorical variety rather than to mark some doctrinal difference in how Jew and Gentile are justified. The real turn is in "make void" (*katargeō*, "render inoperative"): Paul insists faith doesn't cancel the law's authority but is the one thing that finally puts it on solid ground -- a claim he'll spend chapters 4 and 6–8 making good on.
translation: Or is he the God of Jews only? Is he not also of Gentiles? Yes, of Gentiles also -- since God is one, and he will justify the circumcised out of faith and the uncircumcised through faith. Do we then render the law inoperative through this faith? Let it not happen! On the contrary, we establish the law.

label: Romans 4:6–8
text: "Blessed" (*makarios*) in ordinary Greek simply meant fortunate or prosperous; David's declaration repurposes it for a condition entirely apart from circumstance -- a man is "blessed" while still guilty by nature, because the blessing is a credit entry God makes on his account, not a description of his conduct. "Iniquities" is literally "lawlessnesses" (*anomia*), deliberate violation rather than wrongdoing in general, and "are forgiven" pictures those violations formally put away, struck from the record rather than merely overlooked.
translation: Just as David also pronounces the man spiritually prosperous to whose account God credits righteousness apart from works: Spiritually prosperous are they whose lawless deeds were put away and whose sins were covered; spiritually prosperous is the man to whose account the Lord will not credit sin.

label: Romans 4:9–12
text: The order of events in Genesis carries the argument: God credited Abraham with righteousness while he was still uncircumcised, years before the rite was given. Circumcision comes later as a seal stamped onto a righteousness he already possessed, not a condition for earning it. That sequence is what lets Abraham stand as father to both groups -- the uncircumcised who simply believe as he did, and the circumcised who don't merely carry the physical mark but actually walk in the same footsteps of faith he walked while he had no mark at all.
translation: Is this blessing, then, pronounced upon the circumcised, or also upon the uncircumcised? For we say, his faith was credited to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it credited -- while he was circumcised, or uncircumcised? Not in circumcision but in uncircumcision. And he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of the faith he had while still uncircumcised, so that he might become father of all who believe while uncircumcised, that righteousness might be credited to them also -- and father of the circumcised, not to those who are merely circumcised, but to those who also walk in the footsteps of the faith our father Abraham had while he was still uncircumcised.

label: Romans 4:13–15
text: Both key verbs sit in the perfect tense: if the inheritance came through law, faith would stand permanently voided and the promise permanently inoperative -- not set back temporarily but disabled for good. The closing line runs almost like a proof: law's one real product is the possibility of transgression, since a violation requires a standard to violate. Remove the law and the category "transgression" disappears with it, even though sin as a reality does not.
translation: For the promise to Abraham and his offspring, that he should be heir of the world, did not come through law but through the righteousness that comes by faith. For if those who are of the law are the heirs, faith has been rendered void, and the promise has been made permanently inoperative. For the law produces wrath; but where there is no law, neither is there transgression.

label: Romans 4:18
text: The phrase usually smoothed into "against hope believed in hope" actually trades on two different prepositions: his situation lay beyond (*para*) anything nature could offer as grounds for hope, yet he staked his expectation upon (*epi*) hope regardless -- not blind optimism but hope deliberately relocated from natural grounds onto God's word alone.
translation: Who, beyond all hope, believed on the ground of hope, so that he became father of many nations, in keeping with what had been spoken with finality: So shall your offspring be.

label: Romans 4:19–22
text: "Considered" (*katanoeō*) means to look something over carefully, not glance away from it -- the better manuscripts have Abraham staring straight at his situation rather than refusing to face it: a body as good as dead, cast in a perfect tense that pictures a condition already set in and staying set. "Staggered" is literally "to judge between two" (*diakrinō*), the image of a man torn between two verdicts; Abraham reached no such split decision. And "was strengthened" is passive voice -- the strength wasn't something he worked up himself but something worked into him, and it's specifically strength "with respect to faith," not a claim that his body was renewed in advance of the fact.
translation: And not being weak in his faith, he attentively considered his own body, already as good as dead -- he being about a hundred years old -- and the deadness of Sarah's womb besides. Yet at the promise of God he did not waver between two minds in unbelief, but was made strong in his faith, giving glory to God, and being fully convinced that what God had promised, he was able also to perform. Therefore it was credited to him as righteousness.

label: Romans 4:23–25
text: "Shall be imputed" isn't actually future tense in the Greek; it runs on a verb (*mellei*) that expresses a settled, ongoing divine pattern rather than a one-time future event -- closer to "it is credited, and keeps being credited" than "it will be credited someday." "Delivered" (*paradidōmi*) is the verb for handing a prisoner over to the courts -- the Father's act toward the Son is cast in exactly the language of a judicial handover, not a private arrangement between the two. And "offenses" (*paraptōma*) pictures a straying off the path (*para*, "aside," plus the verb "to fall") -- concrete departures from the road, not sin described as an abstract condition.
translation: Now it was not written for his sake alone, that it was credited to him, but for our sake also, to whom it is to be credited -- to us who have faith in him who raised Jesus our Lord from among the dead, who was handed over because of our transgressions, and was raised because of our justification.

label: Romans 5:2
text: "Access" translates prosagōgē, built from a verb meaning "to bring" and a preposition meaning "toward" — the picture is of someone ushering a person into the presence of royalty, securing them an audience and standing there in favor. Paul says believers "have" this access and "stand" in this favor, both in the perfect tense: not a momentary admission but a permanent state, granted once and holding good indefinitely. The hope in view isn't a wish but a settled expectation — the coming glory is itself the guarantee.
translation: Through him we have obtained, and go on holding, our permanent entrance by faith into this favor in which we now permanently stand; and we exult on the ground of the hope of the glory of God.

label: Romans 5:3–5
text: "Glory" here (kauchaomai) means to exult — and Paul says believers exult in tribulations not merely while enduring them but because of them; the hardship itself is the ground of the boasting. "Tribulation" carries the article, marking it as the trouble every believer should expect. The chain that follows runs on a repeating device: tribulation produces endurance (hupomonē, literally "remaining under" pressure rather than escaping it), endurance produces "provenness" (dokimē — not "experience," but the tested, proven character that survives a trial), and provenness produces hope. "Shed abroad" is a perfect-tense verb — the love of God was poured in at one point and floods the heart still, continuing to saturate it.
translation: And not only that — we are continually exulting in our troubles also, knowing that trouble is producing endurance, and endurance, provenness, and provenness, hope; and this hope does not put us to shame, because the love of God has been poured out into our hearts, and keeps on filling them, through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.

label: Romans 5:6–8
text: "For" (huper) does double duty here — "on behalf of" and "instead of." Paul uses the same preposition elsewhere for straightforward substitution, one dying so others need not, and the sense here is the same: Christ died in the place of people who had no reverence for God at all. The timing is called kairos, not just any moment but the fitting, appointed one. Paul then borrows a distinction from ordinary Greek usage, not New Testament theology: the "righteous" man simply meets his obligations, while the "good" man is the generous, warmly regarded one people might actually die for. Even that rare case falls short of what Christ did — he died for enemies, not for the admirable. "Commends" is present tense: God isn't just presenting a past demonstration, he is continually holding this proof up before us.
translation: For while we were still without strength, at the fitting time, Christ died instead of, in behalf of, ungodly men. For someone will hardly die in behalf of a righteous man — though perhaps for the good man someone might even dare to die. But God keeps on demonstrating his own love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died in our behalf.

label: Romans 5:9–11
text: Paul argues from the greater case to the lesser: if God did the harder thing — reconciling enemies — while we were still hostile to him, the easier thing, finishing what he started, is guaranteed. "Wrath" carries the article: not trouble in general but the specific, final judgment. "Enemies" leans toward the passive sense — not simply that we hated God, but that our condition put us at odds with a holy God who could not overlook sin. "Reconciled" (katallassō) means, at root, to exchange — to convert a relationship of hostility into one of peace, and the initiative is God's, not ours; we are the ones acted upon. And where the King James has "atonement," the Greek is really "reconciliation" — the older English sense of "at-one-ment," making two estranged parties one again, not "atonement" in its modern sense of a price paid.
translation: Much more then, having now been declared righteous by his blood, we will be saved through him from the wrath. For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, we will be saved by his life. And not only so, but we also exult in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation.

label: Romans 5:12–14
text: "World" (kosmos) means the human race, the same sense it carries in John 3:16. Paul's picture is that when death entered through Adam, it spread "throughout" every member of the race — the death is universal because Adam functioned as humanity's representative head, so his sin counted as everyone's sin. Paul proves the point from the period between Adam and Moses: there was no written law yet, and sin is not charged to a person's account where there is no law to break — yet people still died. The only explanation is that they died for Adam's sin, inherited through their union with him, not for sins they had individually committed. Adam is called a "type" (tupos), a pattern or mold that foreshadows someone greater to come.
translation: Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin, death, so death spread through to all men, because all sinned. For until law came, sin was in the world, but sin is not charged to one's account where there is no law. Yet death reigned as king from Adam until Moses, even over those who had not sinned after the pattern of Adam's transgression — who is a type of the one who was to come.

label: Romans 5:15
text: "Offense" (paraptōma) pictures a stumble off the path — a departure from where one should be walking. "Free gift" (charisma) is a favor granted with no strings of merit attached. Paul isn't just comparing degree here, sin's damage against grace's remedy — he's building an argument from certainty: the character of the God who gives freely is a surer basis for confidence than the certainty of sin and death running back to one man's fall. Both "the one" transgression and "the one" man carry the definite article in the Greek — Paul keeps Adam and Christ each singled out by their singularity.
translation: But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if by the trespass of the one man the many died, much more did the grace of God, and the free gift by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, overflow to the many.

label: Romans 5:16
text: Paul contrasts sources here. Judgment traces back to a single sin as its source and issues in condemnation; the free gift traces back to many transgressions as its source and issues in justification. One point of origin multiplies into one verdict of guilt; a multiplied problem is answered by one verdict of acquittal.
translation: And the gift is not like the effect of the one man's sinning. For the judgment came from one transgression, resulting in condemnation; but the free gift came from many transgressions, resulting in a righteous verdict.

label: Romans 5:17
text: The weight of the sentence falls on "reigned" — sin's dominion is pictured as a king ruling through death. Paul's logic demands that the second Adam's effect cannot fall short of the first Adam's: if death reigned as king through one man's fall, then those who receive the abundant grace God offers will all the more certainly reign as kings themselves, through the life that comes by the one man, Christ.
translation: For if, by the trespass of the one, death reigned as king through that one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign as kings in life through the one, Jesus Christ.

label: Romans 5:18
text: Paul distinguishes two related but different words: dikaiōma, the righteous deed itself — Christ's act of satisfying what the law demanded — and dikaiōsis, the legal verdict, God's declaration that acquits a person and grants them standing before him. That verdict is described as belonging to life — a genitive that describes its quality, not merely its result: an acquittal bound up with the gift of life itself. Legally, a verdict changes standing, not character; but Paul's phrase shows the verdict here is inseparable from an actual impartation of life to the one acquitted.
translation: So then, as through one trespass the result for all men was condemnation, so also through one righteous act the result for all men is a righteous standing that carries life with it.

label: Romans 5:19
text: "Disobedience" (parakoē) is built from the verb "to hear" plus a prefix meaning "alongside" — literally a hearing that goes astray, an inattentive or careless hearing that shades into refusal. "Obedience" (hupakoē) is built the same way but with a prefix meaning "under" — a hearing that places itself under authority, a willing submission to what it hears. Paul's word for "made" (kathistēmi) is not the ordinary word for manufacturing something, like shaping wood into a spear; it means to appoint or constitute someone to a position by an official, judicial act. By Adam's one act of not-listening, the race was judicially constituted sinful; by Christ's one act of listening and submitting, all who believe are judicially constituted righteous.
translation: For just as through the one man's disobedience the many were constituted sinners, so also through the one man's obedience the many will be constituted righteous.

label: Romans 5:20
text: "Law" here has no article — Paul means law as a method or principle of God's dealing, not the Mosaic code as a specific document. "Entered" (pareiserchomai) is a compound built from "come," "into," and "alongside" — the law didn't originate the problem, it came in alongside a sin already present, to expose it. "Abound" (pleonazō) means to increase or multiply — the law's effect was to multiply transgression by giving the already-rebellious nature something concrete to defy. But grace's response uses a different, stronger compound, huperperisseuō — not just "abound" but "super-abound," to go over and beyond even that increase.
translation: Now law came in alongside, in order that the trespass might be multiplied; but where sin was multiplied, grace super-abounded, and more besides.

label: Romans 5:21
text: "Reigned" (basileuō) again pictures sin as an enthroned king, and the phrase "unto death" describes the sphere in which that reign is carried out and displayed — death is the territory sin rules. Paul sets grace up as the counter-king, ruling not through death but through righteousness, and its rule issues in eternal life, made available through what Christ did.
translation: In order that, just as sin reigned as king in the sphere of death, so also grace might reign as king through righteousness, resulting in eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

label: Romans 6:2
text: Paul's argument in this chapter hinges on a small grammatical fact: "sin," appearing as a bare noun without the article, points to the sinful nature itself rather than to individual sinful acts — the same personified, enthroned power described as "reigning" back in 5:21. The question "shall we continue in sin" uses a present tense that asks about an ongoing, habitual relationship, not an isolated lapse. Paul's answer is that believers "died" to that nature — an aorist verb, apethanomen, built from a root meaning "to die" plus a prefix meaning "away from" — describing a single, completed, unrepeatable severing, not a gradual fading. "Baptized" is simply transliterated rather than translated, and its everyday Greek use (a smith plunging hot iron into water to temper it, a soldier dipping his spear in blood) points to a decisive change of condition through immersion into something new — here, into Christ's own death, so that the believer's tie to the old ruling power is cut at the root.
translation: What then shall we say? Are we to go on remaining in sin, that grace may increase? Away with the thought! How shall we, who died once for all to sin, still go on living in it? Do you not know that all of us who were plunged into Christ Jesus were plunged into his death? We were therefore buried together with him through this plunging into his death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from among the dead through the Father's glory, so we too might order our conduct in newness of life.

label: Romans 6:5–7
text: "Planted together" translates a word (sumphutoi) built on the idea of two things growing up joined, sharing one life between them — Paul pictures the believer's union with Christ's death as organic, not merely legal. "Likeness" (homoiōma) is a resemblance so close it nearly collapses into identity. Two further word choices matter: the "old man" uses palaios, "old" in the sense of worn out through use, not archaios, "old" in the sense of ancient — Paul means the used-up former self, fit to be discarded, not simply a self from long ago. And "destroyed" translates katargeō, which doesn't mean annihilated but rendered inoperative, put out of commission — the body once run by the sinful nature is taken off that nature's payroll, no longer bound to answer its orders.
translation: For if we have grown into permanent union with him in the likeness of his death, we shall also be in the likeness of his resurrection — knowing this, that our old, worn-out self was crucified with him once for all, in order that the body ruled by sin might be put out of commission, so that we should no longer be rendering sin a slave's habitual obedience. For the one who has died stands free, once for all, from sin's claim.

label: Romans 6:8–10
text: "With him" describes the source the believer's life is now drawn from — not fellowship in some vague sense, but ongoing dependence on Christ's own resurrection life for as long as that life continues, which is forever, since death no longer holds any claim over him. "He died to sin once" uses the aorist again — a single, unrepeatable event, done and settled — over against a death that keeps recurring. Since Christ's death dealt with sin's power once for all and his life continues without end, the believer's connection to that life is equally secure and equally permanent.
translation: Now if we died together with Christ, we believe that we shall also go on living together with him, knowing that Christ, having been raised from among the dead, no longer dies; death no longer lords it over him. For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God.

label: Romans 6:11–14
text: "Reckon" (logizomai) is an accounting term — to count something as a settled fact and act on that basis, not to talk yourself into feeling something. Paul tells believers to reckon themselves dead to sin and alive to God as a fact already accomplished by God, not a feeling to manufacture. "Let not sin reign" uses a present imperative with a negative that specifically halts an action already underway — better rendered "stop letting sin go on reigning" than a general warning against something not yet happening. "Yield" (paristēmi) shifts tense meaningfully: Paul first uses it to forbid continuing to place the body's members at sin's disposal, then switches to the aorist to command a decisive, one-time presentation of oneself to God. "Instruments" (hopla) is military vocabulary — weapons, not neutral tools — casting the body's members as armament to be wielded in a real conflict.
translation: So also, keep reckoning yourselves to be dead ones with reference to sin, but living ones with reference to God, in Christ Jesus. Therefore stop letting sin go on reigning as king in your mortal body, to obey its cravings; and stop presenting your members to sin as weapons for unrighteousness — but present yourselves, once for all, to God as those alive from the dead, and your members to God as weapons for righteousness. For sin will not lord it over you, since you are not under law but under grace.

label: Romans 6:15
text: The grammar signals a shift from the previous question. In verse 1 the verb is a present subjunctive, asking about a habitual, ongoing pattern of sin; here it switches to an aorist subjunctive, asking about a single, deliberate lapse instead. The objector has downgraded his proposal — not a whole lifestyle of sin, but the occasional, planned exception, on the theory that grace's rule is more lenient than law's. Paul's answer treats that as no better an idea: grace doesn't loosen the reins, it replaces an external code with an internal power that is, if anything, more exacting.
translation: What then? Are we to sin, on one occasion, because we are not under law but under grace? Away with the thought!

label: Romans 6:16
text: The King James "servants" undersells the word doulos, the strongest Greek term for a slave — someone born into servitude, whose will is absorbed entirely into the master's, bound by ties nothing but death can break. Paul's point is that believers have not become masterless; they have changed masters. What had been an involuntary bondage to the sinful nature, inherited and inescapable, becomes a devoted bondage to Christ, taken on willingly because the believer's whole orientation has changed.
translation: Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, slaves you are to the one you obey — whether of sin, resulting in death, or of obedience, resulting in righteousness?

label: Romans 6:17
text: The verb "delivered" (paradidōmi) is passive and describes believers as those handed over into a pattern of teaching, shaped by it, rather than as people who simply received information and agreed with it. Paul's picture is less like handing someone a book and more like pouring metal into a mold — the teaching left its shape on them from the inside, which is why the obedience that follows comes "from the heart" rather than from external pressure.
translation: But thanks be to God that, though you were once slaves of sin, you obeyed from the heart that pattern of teaching into whose mold you were delivered.

label: Romans 6:18
text: "Made free" (eleutheroō) is the standard term for manumitting a slave — a legal release from one owner. But Paul's logic won't allow for an unowned, ownerless freedom; the moment one master's claim ends, another's begins. Liberation from sin is, in the same act, enlistment under righteousness.
translation: And having been set free from sin, you were made slaves to righteousness.

label: Romans 6:21–23
text: "Wages" (opsōnion) is a soldier's term — not a formal salary but rations, the in-kind subsistence handed out to keep a fighting man alive and able to serve. Paul's picture of sin as a commanding officer doling out rations to its troops is grim: the "pay" it hands out, keeping its slaves going day to day, terminates in death. Against that he sets charisma, the free gift — nothing earned, nothing doled out as compensation for service, simply given.
translation: What fruit then were you having at that time, from the things you are now ashamed of? For the end of those things is death. But now, having been set free from sin and made slaves to God, you are having your fruit resulting in holiness, and the end, eternal life. For the wages sin pays out is death; but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

label: Romans 7:4
text: “Are become dead” translates *thanatoō*, not the plainer “died” Paul used back in chapter 6, but a stronger verb meaning “put to death”—a violent death, not a quiet one. He reaches for the sharper word on purpose: the believer's death to the law didn't happen gently, it happened by the same violence that killed Christ, because it happened *in* Christ's death. The mechanism named is “through the body of Christ”—his actual crucified body is what discharges the believer from the law's claim, the way a wife is released from her husband's law only by his death. The purpose clause that follows completes the picture: death first, then a second marriage, entered so that fruit might be produced for God—not law-keeping, but fruit-bearing.
translation: So that, my brothers, you also were put to death, with violence, with reference to the law, through the body of Christ, resulting in your belonging to another, to him who was raised up out from among the dead, in order that we might go on bearing fruit to God.

label: Romans 7:5
text: “In the flesh” here doesn't mean “in a body”; it names a condition, total captivity to the fallen nature, the opposite number to “in the Spirit” a chapter later. The “motions of sins” translates *pathēma*, a word for stirred passions or impulses, not neutral instincts but sin already active and pressing for release. “Did work” is *energeō*, the ordinary verb for a force actively operating—the law didn't create these impulses, it triggered them into motion. And the fruit that impulse produced wasn't merely followed by death; the phrasing makes it belong to death, death's own crop.
translation: For when we were living in the sphere of the flesh, the sinful passions, which were being stirred up through the law, were continually at work in our body's members, resulting in fruit that belonged to death.

label: Romans 7:6
text: The “dead” in view here isn't the law but the believer's former chained condition—the imperfect tense pictures the evil nature as something that kept holding him down, again and again, before he died with Christ. What follows the discharge isn't a future duty (“that we should serve”) so much as an automatic result: the grammar reports something already happening—present tense, habitual obedience. Paul also reaches for *kainos* rather than *neos* for “new”—not new on the calendar but new in kind, unworn—set against *palaios*, not simply old in years but worn out, obsolete. The contrast running underneath is power source against power source: the Spirit now energizes obedience where the law only ever commanded it and left a person to his own resources.
translation: But now we have been discharged from the law, having died to that in which we were constantly being held down, so that we are habitually rendering a bondslave's obedience in a sphere new in kind, that of the Spirit, and not in a sphere worn out and useless, that of the written code.

label: Romans 7:7
text: “God forbid” translates *mē genoito*, literally “may it not come to be”—the strongest recoil the language allows. Paul's actual answer is that the law didn't create sin, it introduced him to it: the verb for “know” is aorist, marking a coming-to-know by experience at a specific moment, not accumulated head knowledge. The same root, *epithumia*, sits behind both “lust” the noun and “covet” the verb—a craving strong enough to seize the will. And Paul pictures the commandment not as a single utterance but as something that kept on saying, repeatedly, “you shall not desire”—the repeated prohibition itself is what woke the craving up.
translation: What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Away with the thought! But I did not come to know sin experientially, except through the law; for I would not have known evil desire, except that the law kept on saying, You shall not desire.

label: Romans 7:8
text: “Occasion” translates *aphormē*, a term borrowed from military and business language for a base of operations, a staging point for a campaign. Sin didn't originate in the commandment; it commandeered the commandment as its base, using the prohibition itself as leverage to “work,” *katergazomai*, “accomplish fully,” every kind of craving. Before that, sin was “dead”—not nonexistent, but dormant, lacking the friction it needed to spring into action.
translation: But sin, seizing a base of operations through the commandment, worked in me every kind of craving. For apart from law, sin lies dead.

label: Romans 7:9
text: The “life” Paul claims before the law arrived isn't spiritual life—it's the unreflective ease of someone who hasn't yet met a command he could break. The verb behind “revived” is built on the word for “life” with “again” prefixed: sin didn't simply appear when the commandment came, it came back to life, as though sleeping and needing only a prohibition to rouse it. And the “death” that follows isn't physical—it's the collapse of that earlier, unexamined flourishing into misery.
translation: And I was once alive, apart from law. But when the commandment arrived, sin sprang back to life, and I died.

label: Romans 7:10–11
text: The Greek adds an emphatic “this very one” that smoother translations drop—Paul isn't just reporting an outcome, he's marking his own surprise at it: the commandment whose whole aim was life turned out, in his hands, to lead to death. “Was found” is passive, a discovery that happened to him rather than one he went looking for. And the verb for what sin did—rendered “beguiled”—pictures deception: sin used the law's own authority as leverage to talk him into disobedience, then killed him through the very command he had trusted.
translation: And the commandment that pointed to life—this very one, I found, to my surprise, leading to death. For sin, seizing the commandment as its base of operations, deceived me, and through it killed me.

label: Romans 7:12
text: Three separate adjectives are stacked here, not overlapping synonyms: holy names the law's origin in God's own character, righteous its content matching what God requires, good the beneficial end it serves. Piling up all three closes off any reading of the previous verses as an attack on the law itself.
translation: So then, the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, and righteous, and good.

label: Romans 7:13
text: Paul's question—did the good become death to me?—gets the same emphatic refusal as before. His explanation turns on a purpose clause: sin worked death through the good commandment precisely so that sin might be exposed as sin, unmasked for what it actually is. The closing phrase pushes further, into something like “sinful to an extreme degree”—the commandment's role wasn't to make sin worse, but to reveal, using the best possible material, just how bad sin already was.
translation: Did then that which is good become death to me? Away with the thought! But sin, in order that it might be shown to be sin, was producing death in me through what is good, so that sin, through the commandment, might become sinful beyond measure.

label: Romans 7:14–15
text: Paul had three separate words available for describing a person, and the choice here matters: not the “natural” man ruled by reason and appetite with no spiritual life at all, not the “spiritual” man walking in the fullness of the Spirit, but the “fleshly” man—a believer who still, in practice, lives under the old nature's pull. “Sold” is a perfect-tense verb, describing not a past event but a settled, standing condition, a debt already foreclosed. And “know,” in “what I do, I do not know,” isn't intellectual assent but experiential understanding—Paul is saying his own actions have gone opaque to him, explainable only by a pull working against his own best desires.
translation: For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am fleshly, sold, and standing sold, under sin. For what I am doing, I do not understand; for what I want to do, this I am not practicing, but what I hate, this I am doing.

label: Romans 7:16–20
text: “Consent” translates *sumphēmi*, “to say together with”—an active agreement, stronger than mere acknowledgment: even in the act of disobeying, some part of Paul sides with the law he's breaking. He also has two Greek words for “good” and reaches for the one meaning moral beauty rather than the one meaning usefulness—naming what's genuinely admirable about the very command he can't keep. When he writes “no longer I,” the pronoun is placed for emphasis: his considered, willing self isn't the one driving the behavior; something has moved in and is operating him from the inside. And the verb for “want” is present tense, a standing, continuous desire always switched on, set against a verb meaning “to lie ready at hand” for “do”—the desire to do good is perpetually available to him, but the doing itself never shows up alongside it.
translation: If then I am doing what I do not want, I am agreeing with the law that it is beautiful and good. So now it is no longer I myself who am doing it, but the sin dwelling in me. For I know that in me—that is, in my flesh—no good thing is dwelling; for the wanting lies constantly ready at hand in me, but the doing of the good does not.

label: Romans 7:21–23
text: Paul upgrades his vocabulary here: “delight” is a stronger word than the “agree with” of the previous verses, describing genuine moral sympathy rather than bare intellectual assent. He locates that gladness in “the inward man,” his rational, moral self—not identical to the new nature received at the new birth, but the part of a person still oriented toward God. Against it he sets “a different law” operating in his body's members, described in military language: it wages war and takes him prisoner, the verb being the standard one for marching off a captive after a lost battle.
translation: For I delight in the law of God according to the inward man. But I see a different law in my body's members, waging war against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin that is in my members.

label: Romans 7:24–25
text: “Wretched” translates a word that originally described the exhaustion of hard physical labor—not despair as an emotion but the collapse that follows prolonged, fruitless struggle. The Greek word order throws the emphasis onto the pronoun: “wretched man, I”—Paul naming himself first, before the complaint. And when he asks who will deliver him, the interrogative pronoun is grammatically masculine: he isn't asking what method will fix this, he's asking which person will—and framing the question that way already supplies the answer.
translation: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me out of this body of death? Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself, with my mind, am serving the law of God, but with my flesh, the law of sin.

label: Romans 8:1
text: The earliest manuscripts end this verse after “Christ Jesus”—the clause about walking “not after the flesh but after the Spirit” is a later addition, not part of Paul's original sentence. That detail matters for the logic: Paul isn't grounding “no condemnation” in how well a believer behaves, but in his standing—being “in Christ Jesus” names a position, not a performance record.
translation: There is, then, now no condemnation at all for those who are in Christ Jesus.

label: Romans 8:2–4
text: “Law” in verse 2 isn't the Mosaic code but a governing principle—better read “the regulative power of the Spirit, namely, the life that is in Christ Jesus.” That power has already broken the older regulative power of sin and death over the believer, a settled fact rather than an ongoing project. Paul's phrase for the incarnation is built with care: not “in flesh” (too weak a link to sin), not “in the flesh of sin” (too strong, implying Christ shared in sin), but “in the likeness of the flesh of sin”—truly and fully human, wearing sin's own flesh in outward appearance, yet himself without sin. The single preposition behind “for sin” carries the whole weight of the mission, everything done in relation to sin to atone for it and break its hold. And “condemned” names something the law itself never had power to do: the law could pronounce a verdict, but only Christ's death could depose sin from its throne. What follows—the law's righteous requirement “fulfilled in us”—is stated in the passive voice: something done in the believer, God's own accomplishment, not human effort.
translation: For the regulative power of the Spirit—the life that is in Christ Jesus—has set you free, once for all, from the regulative power of sin and death. For what the law was powerless to do, weakened as it was through the flesh, God did: sending his own Son in the likeness of the flesh of sin, and concerning sin, he condemned—deposed—sin in the flesh, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be brought to completion in us, who order our conduct not under the domination of the flesh, but under the domination of the Spirit.

label: Romans 8:5–8
text: The verb behind “mind” means to deliberately set one's thinking toward something, a fixed orientation rather than a passing thought. Paul then shifts to the noun form in a construction meaning “the mind possessed by”—the flesh or the Spirit doesn't merely influence the mind, it owns it. The word for “peace” carries its own picture: its root sense is “to bind together what has been separated,” not a calm feeling but a repaired connection. And “subject,” describing what the flesh-dominated mind cannot do toward God's law, is a military term for falling into rank under a commanding officer—such a mind simply refuses the chain of command.
translation: For those who are habitually dominated by the flesh keep setting their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who are habitually dominated by the Spirit, on the things of the Spirit. For the mind possessed by the flesh is death, but the mind possessed by the Spirit is life and a restored peace; because the mind possessed by the flesh is at war with God—it does not fall into rank under God's law, nor is it able to. And those who are in the sphere of the flesh are not able to please God.

label: Romans 8:9
text: The Greek verb already carries its own subject in its ending, so when Paul adds a separate pronoun for “you,” it's there for emphasis, a deliberate contrast with the flesh-dominated people just described. “Dwell” comes from the word for “house” and means more than occupying space—it pictures someone thoroughly at home, settled in and functioning as a resident rather than a guest. And “provided that” translates a conditional particle used for something assumed true, offered as a test rather than a doubt: the indwelling Spirit is the diagnostic that settles which side of the earlier contrast a person is actually on.
translation: But you, you are not in the sphere of the flesh but in the sphere of the Spirit, provided that the Spirit of God is at home, dwelling, in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, this one does not belong to him.

label: Romans 8:10
