text: The “spirit” set against “body” in this verse is the believer's own human spirit, not the Holy Spirit—the contrast only makes sense as the two component parts of a person. The body already carries death in it, a legacy of Adam's sin working itself out physically. But the human spirit is “alive,” and the life-word used isn't just continued existence—it's life with a moral quality attached, shaped by righteousness rather than neutral survival.
translation: But if Christ is in you, the body, on the one hand, is dead because of sin, but the spirit, on the other hand, is alive because of righteousness.

label: Romans 8:11
text: “Quicken” is a compound built directly on the words for “life” and “make”—not resuscitation of what nearly died but the impartation of a new order of life to a body still subject to death. The phrase “out from among the dead,” used of both Christ's resurrection and the believer's coming one, pictures a targeted extraction, pulled out from the general company of the dead rather than simply revived. Paul credits the same Spirit already resident in the believer with performing this future act—present indwelling is the guarantee of future resurrection.
translation: And if the Spirit of the One who raised up Jesus out from among the dead is dwelling in you, he who raised up Christ out from among the dead will also make alive your mortal bodies, through his Spirit who dwells in you.

label: Romans 8:12–13
text: “Debtors” pictures an obligation owed, and Paul's point is that the believer owes nothing to the flesh—the debt has been cancelled. The two conditional clauses that follow both use present-tense verbs describing habitual, ongoing patterns rather than isolated acts: one who habitually lives under the flesh's dominion is already in motion toward death. The verb for “mortify,” reaching back to the same root used in 7:4 for the believer's own death with Christ, describes a continuous, repeated putting-to-death of the body's deeds—an ongoing campaign carried out through the Spirit's power, not the believer's own effort.
translation: So then, brothers, we are debtors—not to the flesh, to go on living according to the flesh. For if you are habitually living according to the flesh, you are on your way to dying. But if by the Spirit you are habitually putting to death the deeds of the body, you will live.

label: Romans 8:14–17
text: Paul has two separate words for “child” elsewhere—one for a born child still under guardians, one for an adult son with full legal standing—and “sons” here is the second: the language of Roman adoption law, where a person became someone's son with full inheritance rights through a formal legal act rather than birth. “Adoption” is literally “son-placing,” a term with no real equivalent in Jewish custom—Paul is reaching for Roman legal vocabulary his readers would recognize. The cry “Abba, Father” repeats the same address in two languages rather than translating one into the other; the doubling itself is the point, a child's instinct to say the word twice. And “bears witness with” is built on the word for testimony plus “together”—two witnesses, the Spirit and the believer's own spirit, independently arriving at, and jointly declaring, the same verdict.
translation: For as many as are being led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God. For you did not receive a spirit of slavery, leading again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption—of son-placing—by whom we cry out, Abba, Father! The Spirit himself bears joint witness with our spirit, that we are children of God; and if children, also heirs—heirs of God, and joint heirs with Christ, provided that we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him.

label: Romans 8:18
text: “Reckon” is an accounting term—Paul isn't reporting a feeling but the result of a calculation, weighing one thing against another and stating the conclusion the math produces. “Worthy” continues the image: the word means literally “weighing as much as,” the language of a scale, and Paul's claim is that present suffering simply doesn't register on the same scale as the coming glory. The preposition behind “in us” points outward, toward or upon—the glory isn't a private internal experience but something directed onto believers from outside, made visible.
translation: For I have calculated that the sufferings of the present time do not weigh as much, are not worthy to be compared, with the glory that is about to be revealed toward us.

label: Romans 8:19–21
text: “Earnest expectation” is a single compound word built from “away,” “head,” and “watch”—the picture is of someone straining forward, head craned out, eyes fixed on one point, attention pulled away from everything else. Paul applies this to creation itself: the word for “creature” means the whole non-rational created order, animate and inanimate together, personified as a watcher waiting for something specific. The verb for how creation “was made subject” to futility is passive, and Paul is careful about the agency behind it—the construction points to God's will as the occasion rather than naming God as the direct actor, keeping the responsibility for the actual subjecting one step removed even while affirming God ordained the outcome. And the hope in “subjected in hope” belongs grammatically to the thing subjected, not to the one who did the subjecting—creation's own hope, written into the very sentence describing its bondage.
translation: For the creation, with head craned forward and eyes fixed, is waiting, patiently and expectantly, for the uncovering of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility—not willingly, but on account of him who subjected it—in hope that the creation itself also will be set free from its slavery to decay, into the freedom that belongs to the glory of the children of God.

label: Romans 8:22–23
text: The compound verbs Paul uses for creation's groaning both carry “together” as a prefix, but the togetherness is among all the parts of creation groaning in unison with each other—the comparison to believers groaning alongside creation comes next, as its own separate clause. “Firstfruits” is a harvest term for the first installment of a crop, guaranteeing the rest is still to come; Paul applies it to the Spirit's present work in believers as a down payment on a fuller inheritance not yet received.
translation: For we know that the whole creation is groaning together and travailing together, until now. And not creation only, but we ourselves also, who have the first installment of the Spirit—we ourselves also groan within ourselves, waiting eagerly for our adoption, the redemption of our body.

label: Romans 8:24–25
text: Paul's phrase is literally “we were saved in hope”—hope named as the sphere salvation currently exists in, not yet fully realized. He builds a small paradox out of the word itself: hope that has already been seen fulfilled stops being hope by definition, since the word only applies to what remains outstanding. And the word behind “patience” isn't passive waiting but an active steadfastness, the capacity to hold up and keep going under a sustained load.
translation: For in hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he already sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it through patient endurance.

label: Romans 8:26–27
text: The verb behind “helps” is a compound built from three pieces—“with,” “over against,” and “take hold”—picturing someone grabbing the other end of a load and lifting it together with the person carrying it, not taking the whole burden away. The weakness in view is specific to prayer: we know the general aim of every prayer but not “the what,” the definite article marking the missing piece as the particular, situation-specific content we can't supply on our own. “Makes intercession” carries the sense of coming upon someone in distress and stepping in on their behalf, a rescue verb rather than a formal petition, and it's paired with groanings that are literally “unspoken”—inarticulate, never becoming language at all.
translation: And in the same way the Spirit also lends a hand with our weakness; for we do not know the particular thing we should pray for, as is necessary, but the Spirit himself comes to our rescue with wordless groanings. And he who searches the hearts knows what the mind of the Spirit is, because he intercedes on behalf of the saints according to God.

label: Romans 8:28
text: The oldest manuscripts split on whether this verse names God explicitly as the one doing the working, or leaves the sentence without a stated agent—either way the sense converges on the same actor. The verb itself is present tense and compound, “working together,” describing an ongoing, continuous process rather than a single guaranteed outcome announced after the fact. And “called” carries its narrower Pauline sense here—not a general invitation extended to everyone but the effective call that actually brings a person to faith, tied to God's own purpose rather than the person's initiative.
translation: And we know that all things are continually working together for good, for those who love God, for those who are the called ones, according to his purpose.

label: Romans 8:29–30
text: “Foreknew” is built from the ordinary word for “know” with “before” prefixed—its plain lexical sense is a prior knowledge, though how far that knowledge extends (bare foresight, or an active choosing) has been argued for centuries and the word's makeup alone doesn't settle it. “Predestined” is more transparent: it's built on the verb for marking out a fixed boundary, with “before” attached—to set fixed limits on something in advance, here the shape a life will eventually take. “Conformed to his image” sets two words carefully side by side: one for outward form expressing an inner reality, and one for a “derived” likeness, the kind of image a coin bears from the die that struck it, or a child bears from a parent—not a coincidental resemblance between two unrelated things. And the chain of verbs running through these verses—foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified—are all in the same simple past tense, including “glorified,” even though the glorification is still future: Paul states it as already settled, certain in God's own accounting before it happens in ours.
translation: Because those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image, the derived likeness, of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified; and those whom he justified, these he also—already—glorified.

label: Romans 8:31–32
text: The “if” here is a fulfilled condition—Paul isn't raising the possibility that God might be for us, he's arguing from the settled fact that he is. “His own Son” uses a word for what belongs to someone as a private, particular possession—not just “a son” but this one, peculiarly and intimately his. And the verb for “give” in “give us all things” is built directly on the word for grace—a gift extended freely, not a payment owed, matching the argument's logic: if the costliest gift is already given, the lesser ones follow as a matter of course.
translation: What then shall we say to these things? Since God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own—his very own—Son, but gave him up on behalf of us all, how will he not, along with him, freely grace us with all things?

label: Romans 8:33–34
text: “Elect” means literally “chosen out”—the word itself pictures a selection made from a larger group. Both rhetorical questions here turn on a logical impossibility rather than an emotional appeal: the same person cannot occupy two contradictory roles at once. God cannot be the one bringing an accusation and the one issuing the justifying verdict simultaneously—the two acts cancel each other out. And Christ cannot be condemning while, in the same breath, he is interceding on the accused person's behalf; the string of verbs describing him—died, raised, seated, interceding—builds a resume that makes condemnation from that quarter simply incoherent.
translation: Who will bring a charge against God's chosen ones? God is the one who justifies. Who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus is the one who died—more than that, who was raised—who is at the right hand of God, who also is interceding on our behalf.

label: Romans 8:35–39
text: “More than conquerors” translates a single compound verb, built by stacking the ordinary word for victory under a prefix meaning “over and above.” Paul isn't claiming a narrow win; he's claiming that the very things threatening to separate believers from Christ's love end up adding to the victory rather than merely failing to stop it. “I am persuaded” is a perfect-tense verb—not a present feeling of confidence but the settled result of a process already completed, a conclusion reasoned to at some point in the past that has stood, unmoved, ever since. And “creature” in the final phrase, “nor any other created thing,” widens the list to its outer limit—every category already named, and then, in case anything was missed, the whole of creation itself, named and excluded.
translation: Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? Just as it stands written: For your sake we are being put to death all day long; we were regarded as sheep marked for slaughter. But in all these things we are coming off more than victorious, through him who loved us. For I have become, and remain, persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor rulers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

label: Romans 9:10–13
text:
The phrase "purpose according to election" translates *hē kat' eklogēn prothesis* (hē kat' eklogēn prothesis) — literally "the according-to-selecting-out purpose," with the prepositional phrase functioning like an adjective bolted onto "purpose." *Prothesis* (prothesis) comes from *protithēmi*, "to set before oneself," the ordinary word for a plan a person weighs out and settles on in advance — not an impulse but a deliberated resolve. *Eklogē* (eklogē) is built on *eklegō*, "to pick out from a group," so the purpose in view is one that operates by selecting, not by rewarding merit already present. Paul's point rides on timing: the twins were chosen and rejected before either had been born or had done a single thing, good or bad — so whatever "election" means here, it cannot be God ratifying a distinction that human conduct had already created.

The verb translated "hated," *miseō* (miseō), ordinarily does mean outright hatred, but set against "loved" in a comparison like this one it works the way the Hebrew idiom does — naming the weaker of two loves rather than active hostility. "Esau I hated" reads more naturally as "Esau I loved less" than as a claim that God bore Esau active malice.
translation: And not only that — when Rebecca also had conceived by one man, our father Isaac — for the children not yet having been born, nor having practiced anything good or bad, in order that the purpose of God, the one according to a selecting-out, might continue standing, not out of a source of works but out of the One who calls, it was said to her: The older shall be servant to the younger; even as it stands written, Jacob I loved, but Esau I loved less.

label: Romans 9:14–16
text:
Paul's reply hinges on two different verb forms of the same promise. The first "I will have mercy" is a plain future indicative — a straightforward prediction of what God will do. The second occurrence, inside the relative clause, shifts to a present subjunctive, and the relative pronoun carries the indefinite particle *an* (an), turning "whom" into "whoever, no matter who." That grammatical shift is the argument in miniature: God isn't naming favorites in advance so much as asserting that mercy will go wherever he decides to send it, and the decision belongs to him alone, not to any claim a person can lodge against him.

"Not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth" names desire and effort, not identity — "willeth" is simple wanting, "runneth" pictures a competitor straining toward a finish line, laboring for the prize. Paul denies that either wanting mercy or working for it secures it; only God's own character as the one who shows mercy does. The opening question — "Is there unrighteousness with God?" — is phrased in Greek with *mē* (mē), the negative that expects the answer no; Paul isn't entertaining the charge, he's dismissing it before he even argues against it.
translation: What then shall we say? There is no unrighteousness present with God — is there? Let it not be! For to Moses he is saying: I will have mercy on whomever I am having mercy on, and I will have compassion on whomever I am having compassion on. So then, it is not of the one who is wanting it, nor of the one who is running for it, but of the God who is showing mercy.

label: Romans 9:19–21
text:
"Resisted" translates a perfect-tense form of *anthistēmi* (anthistēmi), built from *histēmi*, "to stand," plus the prefix *anti*, "against." The perfect tense doesn't describe an ongoing struggle so much as an arrival — a stand against God's will that has been taken and now simply stands, a settled, finished posture of opposition. Paul isn't picturing someone still pushing; he's picturing someone who has already dug in and stayed there.

"Repliest against" is *antapokrinomai* (antapokrinomai), a compound of *apokrinomai*, "to answer," with that same combative *anti* prefix — not a fresh answer but a contradiction thrown back at an answer already given. The objector isn't asking a question; he's talking back. And "O man" is deliberately set opposite "God" in the sentence — small against great, a reminder of scale before the argument even starts.

The clay imagery runs on two separate words. "Lump" is *phyrama* (phyrama), from a verb meaning "to knead into dough" — an undifferentiated mass, not yet shaped into anything in particular. "Vessel" is *skeuos* (skeuos), the ordinary word for any household implement or container, useful precisely because it can be shaped toward one purpose or another out of that same mass. "The thing formed" is *plasma* (plasma) — our word "plastic" descends from it, meaning simply molded material, still pliable in the potter's hands.
translation: You will say to me then: Why is he still finding fault? For who has taken a stand — and holds it — against his purpose? O man, who indeed are you, the one talking back against God? The molded thing will not say to the one who molded it, Why did you make me like this — will it? Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, out of the same lump to make on the one hand a vessel for honor, and on the other a vessel for dishonor?

label: Romans 9:22–24
text:
"Willing to show his wrath" places the emphasis on God's spontaneous character rather than a settled decree — this is what his holiness disposes him to do, not a hidden plan to magnify judgment later. That's exactly why the sentence pivots to longsuffering: God, though so disposed, held back and endured instead of acting on it.

"Vessels of wrath" doesn't mean vessels filled with wrath or built for the purpose of displaying it — it means vessels that belong to wrath, that have, by their own doing, come under it. The participle "fitted," *katartizō* (katartizō), describes a present, ready-made condition — ripe for destruction — without naming who or what produced that condition. Compare "vessels of mercy," where the verb changes to *proetoimazō* (proetoimazō), "prepared beforehand," built with the "before" prefix spelled out explicitly. Verse 23 says plainly whose action this is and that it happened in advance; verse 22 leaves the agency unstated and simply names the result. The asymmetry is deliberate: mercy is traced straight to God's prior act, while wrath is described as an achieved condition, its history left for the reader to trace back to human conduct.
translation: But if, wanting to show his wrath and to make his power known, God bore, with much patient endurance, vessels of wrath, standing ready, ripened for destruction — in order that he might make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared beforehand for glory, even us, whom he called, not only out from among Jews but also out from among Gentiles —

label: Romans 9:27–29
text:
"Crieth" is *krazō* (krazō), a loud, unrestrained cry rather than measured prophetic speech — Isaiah isn't reasoning with Israel here, he's crying out over them. The remnant theme carries the weight of the passage: even if Israel's number rivals the sand of the sea, only a remnant will be saved.

The word rendered "word" in "finishing and cutting short" is *logos* (logos), not a term for a legal decree — it means an utterance or reckoning, closer to "account" than "command." "Remnant" is *hypoleimma* (hypoleimma), simply "what is left over" — the surviving portion after everything else has been cut away, echoing the small company preserved out of a nation otherwise as numerous as sand.
translation: And Isaiah is crying out over Israel: If the number of the sons of Israel should be as the sand of the sea, the remnant will be saved. For the Lord will accomplish his reckoning upon the earth, finishing it and cutting it short. And just as Isaiah has said beforehand: Unless the Lord of hosts had left to us a seed, we would have become like Sodom, and would have been made to resemble Gomorrah.

label: Romans 9:30–33
text:
There's no article before "Gentiles" in the Greek — Paul is speaking of Gentiles as a category, not a specific group. "Followed after" is *diōkō* (diōkō), the verb for running hard after something, chasing it down — the very picture of the earnest pursuit the Gentiles, ironically, weren't engaged in. "Attained" is *katalambanō* (katalambanō), "to seize, lay hold of and make one's own" — righteousness came to those not chasing it, and they simply took hold of it.

Israel gets a different verb for the same idea in verse 31: not *katalambanō* but *phthanō* (phthanō), "to arrive at, reach" — and the negative form says Israel, for all its pursuing, never reached the goal it was chasing. The contrast is exact: those not running arrived; those running never did, because they were running on the wrong track — works instead of faith. "Righteousness" repeats three times across these verses, underlining that this — not ancestry, not law-keeping — is the real question dividing Paul from his kinsmen. The stone Israel stumbled over is Messiah himself, the demand of faith where they expected achievement.
translation: What then shall we say? That Gentiles, the ones not chasing after righteousness, laid hold of righteousness — a righteousness, that is, that is out of faith. But Israel, chasing after a law of righteousness, did not arrive at that law. Because of what? Because they pursued it not out of faith but as out of works. They struck their foot against the stone of stumbling, just as it stands written: Behold, I am placing in Zion a stone that trips, a rock that offends, and the one believing upon him will not be put to shame.

label: Romans 10:2–4
text:
"Zeal of God" is a genitive of description — zeal that takes God as its object, zeal for him — and Paul concedes it freely; his complaint isn't that it's absent but that it's misdirected. That misdirection traces to a word choice in the next clause: "knowledge" here is *epignōsis* (epignōsis), full, accurate, experiential knowledge, not the plainer *gnōsis*. Israel had real zeal running on partial, insufficient knowledge, and partial knowledge sent that zeal down the wrong road.

"Going about to establish" uses *histēmi* (histēmi), "to set up, erect" — the picture is of building something as one's own monument. "Their own" is *idios* (idios): a righteousness that is personally, privately theirs, the product of their own labor rather than a gift received. "Submitted" is *hypotassō* (hypotassō), a military term for taking one's place in rank under a commanding officer — better rendered "subjected themselves." Israel's failure wasn't a lack of effort but a refusal to fall in under God's righteousness instead of erecting their own. "End" translates *telos* (telos), the point at which something reaches its limit and stops being operative — Christ is the terminus of law as a road to righteousness, not one more law added to the pile.
translation: For I am testifying about them that a zeal for God they have, but not according to full, accurate knowledge. For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to erect their own private righteousness, to the righteousness of God they did not subject themselves. For Christ is the end of the law, unto righteousness to everyone who is believing.

label: Romans 10:5–8
text:
Paul quotes Leviticus 18:5, "the man who does the righteousness of the law shall live by it," and the verb underneath "shall live by it" — *zēsetai en autēi* (zēsetai en autēi) — hangs ambiguous between sphere and means: "shall live in it" or "shall live by it." Either way, the demand is achievement — you must do it to live by it — which is exactly why Paul treats law-righteousness as a dead end for anyone trying to be justified by it rather than simply ordering a life already made right by faith.

Against that, "the righteousness of faith" is personified as speaking for itself, freely adapting Deuteronomy 30:12–14 rather than citing it as a legal proof text. "Abyss" translates *abyssos* (abyssos), literally "bottomless," used here for the realm of the dead. The rhetorical questions — who will go up to heaven, who will go down to the abyss — both cash out (Paul spells this out with "that is," *tout' estin*) as absurd errands, since Christ has already come down in the incarnation and already come up in the resurrection; there's nothing left to fetch. "Word" in "the word of faith" is *hrēma* (hrēma), not *logos* — *hrēma* is the specific spoken utterance, the actual words on someone's lips, rather than the larger, comprehensive idea *logos* carries. Salvation isn't a truth to be quested after; it's a message already sitting on the tongue and in the heart.
translation: For Moses is writing that the man who does the righteousness that is of the law shall live by it. But the righteousness that is of faith speaks in this way: Do not say in your heart, Who will go up into heaven? — that is, to bring Christ down; or, Who will go down into the abyss? — that is, to bring Christ up from among the dead. But what does it say? The saying is near you, in your mouth and in your heart — this is the saying of faith, which we are proclaiming.

label: Romans 10:11–13
text:
"Shall not be ashamed" is better rendered "will not be put to shame" — *kataischynō* (kataischynō) carries a Hebrew sense of suffering repulse or defeat, not embarrassment. Paul isn't promising that believers won't feel awkward; he's promising they won't be beaten back, disappointed, left holding nothing after staking their faith on Christ.

"Difference" is *diastolē* (diastolē), from a verb meaning "to draw apart, distinguish" — a plain distinction, and Paul denies there is one between Jew and Gentile ("Greek" standing in for Gentile generally) at the point of faith. "Lord," *kyrios* (kyrios), applied here to Jesus, is the same title the Greek Old Testament uses for the divine name — using it of Christ is itself a claim to his deity, not incidental vocabulary.
translation: For the scripture says: Everyone who is believing upon him will not be put to shame. For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, for the same Lord is Lord of all, being rich toward all who are calling upon him. For whoever calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.

label: Romans 10:18
text:
Paul's question "did they not hear?" is framed to force a "yes" — of course they heard; he isn't wondering, he's ruling out an excuse. He proves it from Psalm 19:4, a text originally celebrating the heavens' wordless testimony to God, now applied to the gospel's spread. "World" renders *oikoumenē* (oikoumenē), the technical term for the settled, civilized world under Roman rule — not the broader *kosmos* — which makes Paul's claim a real, checkable one: by his day the gospel had traveled the empire about as widely as the Jewish diaspora itself.

He follows with a second question: did Israel fail to *understand*? "Know" here is *ginōskō* (ginōskō), knowledge gained through firsthand grasp, not bare information. The question is built with the negative *mē* (mē), which likewise expects "no" — Israel understood perfectly well and has no excuse. Moses had already warned that God would provoke Israel to jealousy through "a no-people" — Gentiles are literally termed a *no-people*, outsiders with no covenant standing, who would nevertheless receive what Israel spurned. Isaiah goes further still, saying God was "found by those not seeking" him — grace arriving before anyone asked.
translation: But I say, Did they not hear? Certainly they did — into all the earth their voice went out, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world. But I say, Did Israel fail to understand? First Moses says: I will provoke you to jealousy by a no-people, by a nation without understanding I will provoke you to anger. And Isaiah is bold enough to say: I was found by those not seeking me; I became revealed to those not asking for me.

label: Romans 10:21
text: The image is of hands held out all day long — a patient, unbroken appeal that keeps offering itself even after repeated refusal. "Disobedient" translates *apeitheō* (apeitheō), literally "not allowing oneself to be persuaded" — a settled refusal to be won over, stronger than simple ignorance. "Gainsaying" is *antilegō* (antilegō), "to speak against," picturing active, deliberate opposition rather than passive neglect. Israel's exclusion, Paul insists, isn't due to missed opportunity; it's willful, talked-back-at-God resistance.
translation: But to Israel he says: The whole day long I stretched out my hands to a people refusing to be persuaded and speaking against me.

label: Romans 11:2–4
text:
"Foreknew" translates *proginōskō* (proginōskō); in its handful of New Testament uses about God, it carries more than advance awareness — it marks a people fixed beforehand as God's own, foreordination rather than mere prediction. That's the weight behind Paul's argument: a nation chosen in eternity cannot simply be discarded in time. "Wot" is *oida* (oida), certain knowledge, not opinion — Paul assumes his readers already hold this fact as settled. The Elijah episode is introduced with an idiom meaning "in the case of" or "in the history of" Elijah, pointing to a known precedent. Elijah's complaint uses *entugchanō* (entunchanō) compounded with *kata* (kata, "against") — literally "to plead against" — and "digged down" is *kataskaptō* (kataskaptō), "to dig under and demolish," siege language turned on Israel's own altars. God's reply is a *chrēmatismos* (chrēmatismos), a divine oracle — an authoritative pronouncement, not a private impression. The seven thousand are marked by a qualitative relative pronoun, "who are of such a sort" — identified not by a headcount but by character: they had not bent the knee to Baal.

Paul then distinguishes *kairos* (kairos) from *chronos* (chronos): not clock-time but a strategic, decisive season — the present moment of Jew-and-Gentile inclusion is one of those hinge-points in God's plan. "Remnant" is *limma* (leimma), from *leipō* (leipō), "to leave behind" — what's left over when the rest falls away. "Election" is *eklogē* (eklogē), "a picking out," and Paul grounds it explicitly in grace rather than merit. "Is" — describing both the remnant's existence and, a moment later, the nature of grace itself — is *ginomai* (ginomai), "to become," a verb of coming-into-being rather than static fact: the remnant has come into permanent existence by grace, and grace, if it required works alongside it, would stop being grace altogether — the two categories cancel each other the moment they're mixed.
translation: God did not thrust away his people, whom he foreordained. Or do you not know with certainty, in the case of Elijah, what the scripture says — how he pleads against Israel: Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have dug down your altars, and I alone am left, and they are seeking my life. But what does the divine oracle say to him? I have kept in reserve for myself seven thousand men, who are of such a sort as have not bent the knee to Baal. So too, then, at this present decisive season, a remnant has come into being according to a choosing grounded in grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works — otherwise grace stops being grace.

label: Romans 11:7–10
text: "Blinded" is *pōroō* (pōroō), literally "to cover with a callus" — a hardening that grows over the heart the way scar tissue grows over skin. "Slumber" is *katanuxis* (katanuxis), a deep insensibility of mind — not drowsiness but a numbness so complete the gospel simply stops registering. The imagery piles up: *trapeza* (trapeza), "table," pictures a settled, feasting prosperity turned into the very trap that catches its owner; *pagis* (pagis) is a hunter's snare for birds and *thēra* (thēra) a hunter's trap for beasts, both describing destruction laid and sprung; *antapodoma* (antapodoma), "repayment," signals that none of this is arbitrary — it's earned consequence. "Bow down" is *sunkamptō* (synkamptō), "to bend together," the posture of captives whose backs are bent low under a load. As with Pharaoh, whose heart hardened itself before God hardened it further, the pattern is self-inflicted first and divinely confirmed second — reject the light long enough, and blindness becomes judgment.
translation: What then? What Israel was continually seeking after, this it did not obtain — but the chosen ones obtained it, and the rest were made calloused, just as it stands written: God gave them a spirit of deep insensibility, eyes for not seeing and ears for not hearing, down to this very day. And David says: Let their table become for them a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a just repayment; let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see, and keep on bending their backs down continually.

label: Romans 11:11
text: The question is set up with the negative *mē* (mē), demanding "no" — Paul isn't wondering, he's shutting a door. The contrast between "stumble" and "fall" carries real weight: a stumble is a stagger you recover from, a fall is a collapse you don't get up from, and Paul insists Israel's rejection of the Messiah is the former, not the latter. *Hina* (hina), which normally marks purpose ("in order that"), functions here more as result — Israel's stumble wasn't aimed at its own ruin, but God turned it, in his providence, into an opening for the gospel to reach the Gentiles, which was in turn meant to provoke Israel's jealousy and draw it back toward the salvation it had refused.
translation: I say then, They did not stumble so as to fall, did they? Certainly not! But by their stumbling, salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to provoke them to jealousy.

label: Romans 11:12
text:
"Diminishing" translates *hēttēma* (hēttēma), a word for defeat and loss, not a shrinking headcount — Israel's problem is a forfeited inheritance, not fewer people. Paul argues from lesser to greater: if Israel's defeat already overflowed into riches for the world, "fullness" — *plērōma* (plērōma), "that which has been filled up, completed" — names Israel's future full restoration, and that completion promises gains far exceeding what the Gentiles have already gained from Israel's failure.

The connecting word is *de* (de), "but," marking a turn in direction rather than *gar* ("for") giving a reason — Paul isn't explaining why Gentiles matter, he's pivoting to his own stake in the matter. "Magnify" is *doxazō* (doxazō), "to glorify" — Paul honors his Gentile ministry by discharging it faithfully, and he does so with an eye toward his own people: the more fruitful his work among Gentiles, the more likely it is to provoke his kinsmen to jealousy. "Provoke to emulation" and "provoke to jealousy" translate the same verb, *parazēloō* (parazēloō) — Paul's Gentile mission is deliberately aimed, in part, at making Israel want back what it walked away from.
translation: Now if their fall means riches for the world, and their defeat and loss means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their fullness mean? But I am speaking to you Gentiles. Since, then, I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I bring honor to my ministry, if somehow I may provoke to jealousy those of my own flesh, and save some of them.

label: Romans 11:15
text: The "if" running through this argument is *ei* (ei), the "if" of a fact already granted, not *ean* (ean), the "if" of a mere hypothesis — Paul is reasoning from something established, better rendered "since" or "given that." Israel's "casting away" is its temporary setting-aside as the channel of salvation, with the Church stepping into that role — a shift that has already brought reconciliation to the world. Israel's future "receiving," by contrast, is pictured as "life from among the dead" — not a gentle improvement but a resurrection-scale reversal, out of a nation's spiritual deadness into life.
translation: For since their rejection means the reconciling of the world, what will their receiving back mean, but life from among the dead?

label: Romans 11:16
text:
"For" here is *de* (de), carrying a continuative "now" rather than a strict causal "for." "First-fruit" points to the patriarchs, drawing on the law of the first portion of dough set apart for the priests (Numbers 15) — a small part offered on behalf of the whole. The "if" is again *ei* (ei), the "since" of an established fact. "Holy" is *hagios* (hagios), "set apart," a status word rather than a claim about moral perfection — the patriarchs' consecration to God carries the whole nation's future along with it: root and branches share the same set-apart standing.

The olive-tree picture that follows is worth noting for how it *breaks* the normal agricultural process rather than following it: ordinarily a cultivated shoot is grafted onto wild rootstock to improve it, but here it's the wild branch — the Gentile — grafted into the cultivated tree, an inversion Paul elsewhere calls "contrary to nature." Natural branches (unbelieving Israel) are cut away; the wild branch draws its life from a root it did not grow. The point of the picture is directional: nourishment flows from root to branch, not the reverse, so the grafted-in Gentile owes everything to the root and has no grounds to look down on the branches broken off beside him.
translation: Now since the first portion is holy, so is the whole lump; and since the root is holy, so are the branches. Now since some of the branches were broken off, and you, a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among them and became a partaker with them of the root and the richness of the olive tree, stop boasting against the branches. But if you do boast — remember, you do not support the root; the root supports you.

label: Romans 11:19–21
text: "Well" translates *kalōs* (kalōs), used here as a term of grudging, partly ironic concession — Paul isn't agreeing, he's letting the objection stand only long enough to correct it. The point he presses is that both being broken off and standing firm are governed by moral conditions, not automatic status: the branches were broken off "because of unbelief," and the one standing now stands "by faith," full stop — no inherited immunity either way. The comparison is corporate throughout — the nation Israel and the Gentile world as collective entities — not a statement about any one believer's grip on salvation. Paul's warning targets presumption in a class of people, unbelieving Gentiles who might coast on privilege, not genuine faith itself: if God did not spare the natural branches for unbelief, he will not spare branches grafted in artificially if they fall into the same unbelief.
translation: You will say then, Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in. Granted. They were broken off because of unbelief, and you stand by faith. Do not be high-minded, but be fearing; for if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you.

label: Romans 11:22
text: "Goodness" is *chrēstotēs* (chrēstotēs), kindness or benignity; "severity" is *apotomia* (apotomia), a word built on the image of something cut off sheer — a cliff-face, an abrupt drop — describing rigor without softness. The condition attached is *ean* (ean), a genuine hypothetical: everything depends on "continuing" — *epimenō* (epimenō), "to remain, to abide," a word often used of a guest staying on in someone's house. It pictures an ongoing relationship of dependence, not a one-time transaction; the Gentile's standing lasts only as long as he keeps abiding in that kindness rather than presuming on it. "Cut off" is literally "cut out," the same pruning image used of the branches removed earlier — a warning that privilege without continuance is no privilege at all.
translation: See then the kindness and the severity of God — severity toward those who fell, but toward you, kindness, provided you keep on abiding in that kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut out.

label: Romans 11:23
text:
"They" is *ekeinos* (ekeinos), "those," a pointed, at-arm's-length pronoun for the unbelieving Jews. The condition is again *ean* (ean), genuinely open — nothing forces their unbelief to continue. Paul's claim that "God is able" assumes not just the possibility but the real difficulty of regrafting what was cut away — restoring a broken branch is a harder feat than grafting in a wild one to begin with.

"Mystery" is *mustērion* (mustērion), a once-hidden plan of God now disclosed to believers, not a puzzle left unsolved. Paul distinguishes two timelines that are easy to blur: the political dominance of Gentile powers over Israel, running from Babylon to the final defeat of Antichrist, and the "fullness of the Gentiles," the completion of the Church, the body gathered from Pentecost onward. Israel's hardening is explicitly partial — "in part" — and time-bound, lasting only until that fullness is reached.

"And thus" describes manner more than sequence — not merely "afterward" but "by this means": through the very jealousy Gentile inclusion was designed to provoke, the nation as a corporate whole will be saved, each living Israelite converted at once at the Messiah's return, fulfilling covenant language about a Deliverer removing Jacob's sin.

Finally, "concerning"/"touching" render *kata* (kata), marking two respects in which God relates to Israel: hostile as measured by their present rejection of the gospel, beloved as measured by his covenant with the fathers. "Gifts" is *charisma* (charisma), a favor given without any merit earning it — a stronger word than the ordinary *dōron* (dōron), "gift." "Calling" is *klēsis* (klēsis), the technical term for God's authoritative summons into his kingdom, not a modern "vocation." And "without repentance" is *ametamelētos* (ametamelētos), built on *metamelomai* (metamelomai), "to change one's mind" — God's gifts and calling to Israel are not subject to a change of his mind; what he has promised the nation remains irrevocably on the books.
translation: And those also, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in; for God is able to graft them in again. For if you were cut out of what is by nature a wild olive tree, and contrary to nature were grafted into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, who are the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree? For I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery, brothers, so that you may not be wise in your own estimation: a hardening in part has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And by this means all Israel will be saved, just as it stands written: Out of Zion will come the Deliverer; he will turn ungodliness away from Jacob. And this is my covenant with them, when I take away their sins. As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake; but as regards God's choice, they are beloved for the fathers' sake. For the gifts and the calling of God are not subject to a change of his mind.

label: Romans 11:30–32
text: "Concluded" (in older English) translates *sugkleiō* (synkleiō), "to shut up on every side, to enclose completely" — a picture of being hemmed in with no way out, not merely grouped together. The verb applies evenly to both Gentile and Jew: each shut up, in turn, under the same charge of unbelief. "Not believed" and "unbelief" both render *apeitheō* (apeitheō), "to refuse to be persuaded" — the same stubborn, willful refusal named back in chapter 10. Paul's structure is deliberately reciprocal: Gentile disobedience once opened the door to mercy through Jewish unbelief; Jewish disobedience now will, in the end, open the door to mercy through the mercy already shown the Gentiles. Nobody gets to claim a merit-based exemption — everybody is shut up under the same disobedience, so that everybody's rescue can only ever be traced to mercy.
translation: For just as you were once disobedient to God, but now have been shown mercy through their disobedience, so also they have now been disobedient, in order that, through the mercy shown to you, they also may now be shown mercy. For God has shut up all people together under disobedience, so that he might show mercy to all.

label: Romans 11:33–36
text: *Anexichniastos* (anexichniastos), translated "unsearchable" and "past finding out," pictures a trail with no scent or footprint left to follow — the same word could describe a bloodhound that loses the trace, or a guide who can't pick out a path through unmarked woods. Paired with *hodos* (hodos), the ordinary word for a road, the phrase says God's ways are a road that can't be traced by walking it backward: human reasoning can follow the argument this far and then the trail runs cold. Paul doesn't answer his own questions — who has known the Lord's mind, who has counseled him, who has ever put him in debt — he lets them stand as rhetorical dead ends. The doxology that follows isn't speculation filling the gap; it's worship: everything traces back to God as its source, moves forward through God as its means, and arrives at God as its goal.
translation: O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who became his counselor? Or who has first given to him, that it should be repaid to him? Because from him, and through him, and to him, are all things. To him be the glory forever. Amen.

label: Romans 12:2
text: "Conformed" translates *sunschēmatizō* (sunschēmatizō), built on *schēma* (schēma), an outward shape put on from outside rather than grown from within, with the prefix *sun*- specifying the pattern being copied: this present age, *aiōn* (aiōn) — not the created world but the shifting climate of thought and fashion current in it at any given moment. The verb is a present imperative with the negative *mē* (mē), a construction that in Greek doesn't forbid starting something but orders the stopping of something already underway: quit letting the age keep pressing you into its mold. Set against it is *metamorphoomai* (metamorphoomai), "transformed" — the very word used of Christ on the mountain, where the glory already His by nature broke through to the surface. Applied to the believer, it isn't a new costume but a different source: an outward expression rising out of a genuinely changed inner life, sustained through *anakainōsis* (anakainōsis), the ongoing renewal of the mind, not a single decision but a continuing overhaul. The purpose clause leans on *dokimazō* (dokimazō), the verb for testing metal to certify it genuine — as the mind is remade, a believer is able to put God's will to the test and find it approved: good, pleasing, and *teleios* (teleios), lacking nothing needed to be whole.
translation: And stop being conformed to this age, but keep on being transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you keep testing and approving what the will of God is — the good and pleasing and complete will.

label: Romans 12:3
text: Paul stacks three verbs on the same root, *phroneō* (phroneō), "to form a judgment, to think." No one is to *huperphronein* (huperphronein) — to over-think himself, the same *huper*- prefix behind our word "hyper," pushing self-estimate past the mark — but rather to *sōphronein* (sōphronein), literally to think within sound limits, from *sōs* ("sound") and *phrēn* ("mind"): a calm, accurately sized self-assessment, which has nothing to do with false modesty and everything to do with getting the number right. The standard for that estimate is introduced by *kata* (kata), "down along, in keeping with" — each believer's gauge is fixed by the measure of faith God apportioned him, not by comparison with somebody else's. Paul immediately backs the point with the body: *praxis* (praxis), a member's function or mode of operating, differs from part to part, yet every part belongs to one body. Sober self-estimate, in other words, isn't self-erasure — it's seeing your one function clearly inside a body that needs all the others too.
translation: For I am saying, through the grace given to me, to everyone among you: do not be thinking more highly of yourself than you ought to be thinking, but be thinking so as to be sound-minded, each one according to the measure of faith God apportioned to him.

label: Romans 12:6–8
text: *Charisma* (charisma) names a grace-gift — an enablement supplied by the Spirit, not a talent a person develops on his own. Prophecy is to run *kata tēn analogian tēs pisteōs*, "according to the proportion of faith" — *analogia* (analogia) was a mathematical term for a fitted ratio, so the gift is to be used in step with the faith given for it, not stretched past it. "Ministry" is *diakonia* (diakonia), active service, and every gift-word in this list sits in the Greek locative of sphere: stay inside the lane your gift defines instead of drifting into someone else's. Giving is to be done with *haplotēs* (haplotēs), "singleness" — no double motive hiding behind the gift, no strings attached. Leading belongs to *ho proistēmi* (ho proïstēmi), literally "the one stationed out in front," and it's to be carried out with *spoudē* (spoudē), the zeal of someone who hurries rather than drags his feet. And showing mercy takes *hilarotēs* (hilarotēs) — our word "hilarity" comes straight from it — mercy shown with warmth, not the grudging duty of a chore checked off.
translation: Having gifts differing according to the grace given to us: whether prophecy, let it be in proportion to the faith; or service, let it be within the service; or the one teaching, within the teaching; or the one exhorting, within the exhortation; the one sharing, with singleness of purpose; the one leading, with eager diligence; the one showing mercy, with cheerful readiness.

label: Romans 12:9–13
text: *Anupokritos* (anupokritos), "without hypocrisy," comes from the verb for an actor taking a part on stage — the love commanded here has no script and no performance in it. The hatred owed to evil is *apostugeō* (apostugeō), built on a root for hatred that shows itself openly rather than one nursed quietly out of sight, with *apo*- added to press the sense of pulling away, putting real distance between yourself and it. What you hold onto instead takes *kollaō* (kollaō), the verb for gluing something fast — stick to the good the way glue bonds two surfaces. Family warmth inside the church runs on *philostorgos* (philostorgos), built on the verb for the instinctive love of kin: Paul asks believers to feel toward one another the pull that blood relatives feel. Zeal is to *zeō* (zeō), "boil," and the definite article marking "spirit" here points to the Holy Spirit rather than mere human enthusiasm — the fuel matters as much as the heat. Endurance is *hupomenō* (hupomenō), literally "remain under" — staying put beneath the pressure instead of looking for the exit — and prayer takes *proskartereō* (proskartereō), the word elsewhere used of a soldier's constant post and the apostles' unbroken devotion to prayer. Hospitality gets the strongest verb of the set, *diōkō* (diōkō), "pursue, chase after" — not waiting for a need to knock but going out looking for the chance to meet one.
translation: Love — without acting a part. Be constantly abhorring what is evil, sticking fast to what is good. In brotherly love, be devoted to one another with family affection; in showing honor, be outdoing one another. In zeal, not lagging; boiling in the Spirit; serving the Lord as opportunity comes. Rejoicing in hope; enduring under affliction; persevering unremittingly in prayer; sharing as your own in the needs of the saints; pursuing hospitality.

label: Romans 12:14–16
text: "Bless" is *eulogeō* (eulogeō), literally "to speak well" (*eu* + *legō*) — our word "eulogy" is this Greek word carried over whole. It's a present imperative ordering a settled habit: keep speaking good over the very people persecuting you. "Curse," *kataraomai* (kataraomai), gets the opposite construction — a present imperative with the negative, which in Greek stops something already in motion rather than warning against its start. Paul isn't guarding against a future temptation; he's telling them to quit a habit some already had. "Condescend" translates *sunapagō* (sunapagō), a passive verb meaning to be carried along together with something — not stooping down to lowly people from a position of height, but letting yourself be swept into their company by the same current they're in. And "in your own conceits" is literally "with yourselves" — wisdom measured against no standard but your own opinion of yourself, a private court where you sit as both defendant and judge.
translation: Be constantly blessing those who are persecuting you; be blessing and stop cursing. Be rejoicing with those who rejoice, be weeping with those who weep. Be of the same mind toward one another; not setting your mind on the high things, but being carried along together with the lowly. Stop being wise in your own estimation.

label: Romans 12:19–21
text: "Avenge" is *ekdikeō* (ekdikeō), "to assert one's own right," and once again the construction is a present imperative with the negative — an order to end something already underway: stop taking your own justice into your own hands. In its place, "give place to wrath" — the definite article marks a specific wrath, God's — meaning leave the space empty rather than crowding in to do His job for Him. The repayment verb, *antapodidōmi* (antapodidōmi), stacks two prepositions onto "give" to intensify it into "pay back in full," and that full reckoning belongs to God alone. The coals-on-the-head image draws on an everyday hardship: a hearth fire gone out meant walking to a neighbor and carrying home borrowed embers in a container balanced on the head. Handing an enemy a generous supply of coals wasn't cruelty — it met a real, humbling need and could turn hostility into gratitude. The chapter closes with a matched pair of present imperatives, "stop being conquered" by evil and "keep on conquering" evil with good, putting the believer on the offensive rather than the defensive.
translation: Stop avenging yourselves, beloved, but leave room for the wrath; for it stands written, Vengeance belongs to me, I will repay in full, says the Lord. But if your enemy hungers, be feeding him; if he thirsts, be giving him drink; for in doing this you will be heaping coals of fire upon his head. Stop being overcome by evil, but keep on overcoming evil with good.

label: Romans 13:2
text: The one who "resists" is described with a middle-voice participle of *antitassō* (ἀντιτάσσω) — the picture isn't of resistance done to him but resistance he stages himself: he arranges himself in battle order against the authority, like troops drawn up for a fight he started. What he has thereby done to God's ordinance is put in a different verb, *anthistēmi* (ἀνθίστημι), and it's perfect tense — not "he opposed" as a completed past act but "he stands opposed," a settled, ongoing condition he has put himself into and continues to occupy. "Judgment" translates *krima* (κρίμα), the plain word for a judicial sentence handed down by a magistrate — Paul pictures an actual verdict, not a vague cosmic comeuppance.
translation: So that the one who is arraying himself in battle against the authority has set himself in permanent opposition to the ordinance of God; and those who are so opposing shall receive judgment for themselves.

label: Romans 13:5–7
text:
Paul grounds submission on two supports at once: the external threat of wrath, and the internal witness of conscience — the believer obeys not merely because refusal is dangerous but because something in him agrees with the arrangement. "Pay" translates *teleō* (τελέω), "to fulfill, complete" — it casts tax payment as the completion of an obligation already owed, not a favor granted. The verb form is grammatically ambiguous between statement and command, and most take it as a plain statement of fact: submission is already settled for the Christian, and paying taxes simply follows from it. "Tribute" is *phoros* (φόρος), literally "that which is brought in."

The word for "minister" changes between verse 4 and verse 7. There it was *diakonos* (διάκονος), a servant considered in what he does. Here it's *leitourgos* (λειτουργός), the word used elsewhere for the sacred service of priests in the temple — Paul quietly elevates the magistrate's office into the category of divinely appointed service. "Render" is *apodidōmi* (ἀποδίδωμι), the simple verb "give" with a prefix meaning "off, away from" — paying something out of a reserve one holds, discharging a debt rather than making a gift. "Dues" (*opheilē*, ὀφειλή) is the ordinary word for a debt, carrying real moral weight — what is owed, not merely requested.
translation: On account of this there is a necessity to keep on subjecting oneself, not only because of the wrath but also because of the conscience — for because of this you keep on paying the taxes, for they are God's public servants, continually devoting themselves to this very thing. Pay off to all what is owed: to the one collecting tax, the tax; to the one collecting toll, the toll; to the one who is owed fear, fear; to the one who is owed honor, honor.

label: Romans 13:8
text: "Owe no man anything" is a present imperative with the negative *mē* (μή) — grammatically this doesn't forbid ever incurring a debt, it forbids the continuation of one already running. Paul isn't outlawing loans; he's telling people who owe money to settle up. The one debt he deliberately exempts is love — the kind the Spirit produces in a believer, self-giving toward the person loved. Unlike every other debt, this is one that grows the more it's paid: discharging it doesn't cancel it, it deepens the capacity for more.
translation: Stop owing to even one person, even one thing — except to be continually loving one another. For the one who is loving another has fulfilled the law.

label: Romans 14:4
text: "Who art thou" opens with the pronoun thrown forward for emphasis — Paul stops the weaker believer short: you, of all people, judging someone else's household slave (*oiketēs*, οἰκέτης, a servant belonging to a household, not a hired hand)? The force of the word is ownership — this person answers to a master, and that master isn't you. Whether he "stands or falls" is settled by that relationship, not by a fellow servant's verdict. The best manuscripts read "Lord" rather than "God" here, keeping the focus specifically on the believer's relation to Christ as owner. The closing verb is passive and confident — he *shall be made* to stand — the guarantee rests on the master's power to keep him upright, not on the servant's own strength.
translation: As for you — who are you, judging another's household slave? To his own master he stands or falls. And he shall be made to stand, for the Lord has the power to make him stand.

label: Romans 14:5
text: "Alike" in most English renderings of this verse has nothing behind it in the Greek — drop it and the sense sharpens: the man who esteems every day is subjecting each day, one by one, to his own moral scrutiny. "Fully persuaded" translates *plērophoreō* (πληροφορέω), a word built around the idea of being carried to full measure — not a shaky opinion but a complete, settled conviction. Paul's point in both directions is that the conviction has to be one's own, arrived at personally rather than borrowed from someone else.
translation: The one, on the one hand, is judging one day above another day; the other is subjecting every day alike to his scrutiny. Let each one be fully assured in his own mind.

label: Romans 14:6
text: "Regards" translates *phroneō* (φρονέω), a word for the whole cast of mind, not a bare opinion — how someone thinks and feels about a matter together. "To the Lord" puts *kurios* (κύριος) in the dative as a dative of reference: the man's verdict on the day is rendered with the Lord as the standard he's measuring against. The same construction governs the eater and the abstainer — each one's practice is oriented toward Christ, and each backs it with thanksgiving, which is Paul's proof that both, done in faith, land on the same target.
translation: The one who is regarding the day, with reference to the Lord he regards it. And the one who is eating, with reference to the Lord he is eating, for he gives thanks to God; and the one who is not eating, with reference to the Lord he is not eating, and he gives thanks to God.

label: Romans 14:7–9
text: "To himself," "to the Lord" run through these verses as the same dative of reference each time — a life, and a death, is always lived with reference to someone, and Paul's claim is that for the believer that someone is never the self. The verb for Christ's "reviving" is simply *zaō* (ζάω), "to live," but here it's aorist — a completed, punctiliar act rather than an ongoing state — and the word order points it at the resurrection specifically, not at his years walking the earth. That distinction matters for the purpose clause that follows: Christ died and was raised in order that (a genuine *hina*-purpose clause) he might exercise lordship — the verb is *kurieuō* (κυριεύω), "to rule as *kurios*" — over both the dead and the living. His death and resurrection weren't merely an event in his own biography; they secured a rule that now covers everyone, on either side of the grave.
translation: For not one of us is living with reference to himself, and not one is dying with reference to himself. For if we live, with reference to the Lord we live; and if we die, with reference to the Lord we die. Whether then we live or we die, we belong to the Lord. For to this end Christ died and lived again, in order that he might rule as Lord over both dead ones and living ones.

label: Romans 14:10–12
text: "Thou" is emphatic again, echoing verse 4 — Paul circles the same pronoun back at both sides now, weak and strong alike, for judging and for despising each other. The best manuscripts read "judgment seat of God," not "of Christ," keeping the scene deliberately cosmic. "Confess" is *exomologeō* (ἐξομολογέω), "to acknowledge from the heart" — every knee bowing and every tongue confessing here isn't grudging admission, it's praise wrung out of everyone alike. "Give account" renders the standard bookkeeping idiom for closing a ledger — everyone settles their own account, personally, with no one else's column to answer for.
translation: But you — why are you judging your brother? Or you again — why are you despising your brother? For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of God. For it stands written: As I live, says the Lord, to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall confess to God. So then each one of us shall give account concerning himself to God.

label: Romans 14:13
text: "Let us not judge" is present tense — Paul isn't forbidding a single verdict, he's telling the church to break a running habit of criticizing each other. He then pivots the same word to a better use: judge this instead. "Stumbling block" is *proskamma* (πρόσκαμμα), built on the verb "to strike against" — the image is a stone or obstacle in the road that catches someone's foot. "Occasion to fall" is a different word, *skandalon* (σκάνδαλον), originally the trigger-stick of a trap — not just something you trip on but something engineered to catch you. Paul moves from a passive hazard to an active snare within a single sentence.
translation: Therefore let us no longer be judging one another; but judge this instead — not to be placing a stumbling block before your brother, or a trap in which he may be caught.

label: Romans 14:14
text: "I know" is *oida* (οἶδα), flat, absolute knowledge, no qualification attached. "Am persuaded" shifts to *peithō* (πείθω) in the perfect tense — not "I became convinced" but "I have arrived at conviction and stand there still," a finished process with a permanent result. "Unclean" translates *koinos* (κοινός), "common" — the word doesn't mean dirty or immoral, it means undistinguished from ordinary use, the opposite of *hagios* (ἅγιος), "set apart." Nothing is *koinos* in itself; the category is ceremonial, not moral. And Paul roots the conviction "in the Lord" — not a private opinion he reasoned his way to, but a settled certainty that belongs to him as a Christian, held in Christ.
translation: I know — with absolute knowledge — and stand persuaded in the Lord Jesus, that nothing is common in itself; only to the one who reckons a thing to be common, to that one it is common.

label: Romans 14:15
text: "Meat" is the generic word *brōma* (βρῶμα), "food" — not flesh specifically, whatever the strong believer is eating over his brother's objection. "Made to grieve" doesn't require that the weaker believer be talked into eating against his own conscience — it can simply mean the distress of watching someone he respects do something his own conscience can't approve. Either way, Paul treats causing that pain as already a breach of love. "Destroy" is *apollumi* (ἀπόλλυμι), "ruin" — a strong word, deliberately jarring, applied to a person for whom Christ died, over something as small as a meal.
translation: For if because of food your brother is being grieved, you are no longer walking according to love. Stop ruining, by your food, the one on behalf of whom Christ died.

label: Romans 14:16–18
text: "Evil spoken of" is *blasphēmeō* (βλασφημέω) — reviled, given a bad name; Paul warns that careless use of freedom can get something genuinely good slandered. "The kingdom of God" here isn't "eating and drinking" (*brōsis kai posis*, βρῶσις καὶ πόσις) but righteousness, peace, and joy — and none of the three carry their usual theological weight in this context. Righteousness is practical uprightness toward other people, not justification; peace is concord between believers, not peace with God; joy is the shared gladness that grows out of a community not at war with itself — and all three are located "in the Holy Spirit," his product, not human effort. "Serve" is *douleuō* (δουλεύω), slave-service — total, not occasional. "Acceptable" (*euarestos*, εὐάρεστος) is what pleases God; "approved" (*dokimos*, δόκιμος) is a metals term, the stamp put on something tested and passed.
translation: Therefore stop letting your good be spoken of as evil. For the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. For the one who in this is serving Christ as a slave is well-pleasing to God, and approved — having been tested and stamped so — by men.

label: Romans 14:19
text: "Follow" is *diōkō* (διώκω), "pursue" — the word for a hunt or chase, not a stroll. Whether it's a command ("let us pursue") or a statement ("we are pursuing") turns on a single letter in the Greek manuscripts, an omega versus an omicron — a point where textual criticism runs out and the surrounding grammar has to decide it. Since the next verse switches to a flat imperative, the exhortatory reading fits the flow best. "Edify" is *oikodomeō* (οἰκοδομέω), literally "build a house" — construction language for growing someone in grace. "One another" carries a defining article in the Greek easy to lose in translation: Paul means building up specific individuals in the room, not a vague corporate mass.
translation: So then, let us be eagerly pursuing the things of peace, and the things that build up — with reference to one another.

label: Romans 14:20
text: "Destroy" here isn't the word from verse 15 (*apollumi*, "ruin"); it's *kataluō* (καταλύω), "tear down" — the demolition word, set deliberately against *oikodomeō*, "build up," from the previous verse. Paul pictures a building crew undoing its own work over a meal. "Pure" (*kathara*, καθαρά) keeps the same ceremonial sense running through the chapter — nothing here is a moral judgment on the food itself. "With offense" describes not what's eaten but how: eating in a way calculated to become a stumbling block to someone watching.
translation: Stop tearing down the work of God for the sake of food. All things indeed are pure — but it is evil for the man who is eating so as to cause offense.

label: Romans 14:21
text: "Flesh" here is *kreas* (κρέας), and in this setting it points specifically to meat with a compromised pedigree — the kind that had passed through pagan sacrificial use — not meat in general. Wine and this kind of meat were the two concrete points of the weaker believer's scruple, and Paul's counsel narrows to match: better to forgo either, or anything else that trips a brother, than to insist on the right to have it.
translation: It is good not to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor to do anything by which your brother stumbles.

label: Romans 15:4
text: "That" translates *hina* (ἵνα), a genuine purpose clause — Scripture wasn't written by accident for later readers, it was aimed at them on purpose, "for our learning." "Comfort" is *paraklēsis* (παράκλησις), a wide word built on "calling alongside" — it covers everything from exhortation to consolation to encouragement, whatever help a person in need requires, not just soothing. Paul pairs it with patience as the twin products Scripture is meant to produce, both feeding into hope.
translation: For whatever things were written beforehand were written for our instruction, in order that through the patience and through the encouragement that comes from the Scriptures we might keep on having hope.

label: Romans 15:5–7
text: "That" (*hina*) again marks purpose: the unity Paul prays for isn't the goal itself, it's aimed at something further — glorifying God with one voice. The little word sometimes rendered "even" is just *kai* (καί), ordinary "and," and the better reading treats it plainly: "the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ," naming God specifically as the Father of Jesus, the same construction Paul uses elsewhere. "Receive" is *proslambanō* (προσλαμβάνω) in the middle voice — "take to oneself," the language of drawing someone into one's own circle, granting them access to one's heart. The standard Paul sets is Christ's own reception of each believer — no lower bar is available for how they're to receive one another.
translation: Now may the God of the patience and the encouragement give to you to be of the same mind with one another according to Christ Jesus, in order that with one accord, with one mouth, you may keep on glorifying the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore keep on taking one another to yourselves, just as Christ also took us to himself, for the glory of God.

label: Romans 15:10–12
text: "Root" translates *riza* (rhiza) — not the trunk or branch but the sprout that pushes up out of the root system, the lowest and least visible part of the plant. The picture in Isaiah's quotation trades on that contrast: what comes up out of the hidden root of Jesse's line rises to become the standard the nations rally to. And the verb Paul chooses for the Gentiles' response is not the ordinary New Testament word for believing, *pisteuō* (pisteuo), but *elpizō* (elpizo), "to hope" — the Gentiles are pictured fixing their hope on this shoot from Jesse's root, setting up the theme Paul immediately develops in verse 13.
translation: And again he says, Be glad, Gentiles, with his people. And again, Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples praise him. And again Isaiah says, There will be a sprout out of the root of Jesse, even the one who is rising up to rule the Gentiles — on him will the Gentiles set their hope.

label: Romans 15:13
text: "In believing" renders a present infinitive with the article, *en tōi pisteuein* (en to pisteuein) — literally "in the believing," picturing faith not as one decisive act but as an ongoing, habitual exercise. The joy and peace Paul prays for rest on that continuous believing, not on a memory of it. "Abound" is *perisseuō* (perisseuo), built on the idea of exceeding a fixed measure — the related noun *perissos* (perissos) means "more than necessary, superadded." Paul is not praying for enough hope to get by; he is praying for a surplus, hope running over the rim. And "Ghost" here is simply older English for *pneuma* (pneuma), "spirit" — no different sense from "Spirit" elsewhere.
translation: Now may the God of hope keep filling you with all joy and peace in the continual believing, so that you keep overflowing with abundant hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.

label: Romans 15:14
text:
Paul's "I am persuaded" is a perfect tense — not a passing impression but a settled conviction reached and still held: "I have been thoroughly persuaded, and stand persuaded still." "Ye yourselves" is emphatic in the Greek, stressing that the Roman believers are full of goodness in their own right, not because Paul coached them into it. "Filled" is likewise perfect tense — completely filled, with that fullness continuing — and "all knowledge" means the whole range of Christian understanding, not omniscience.

His claim to have "written" boldly is an epistolary aorist, a first-century courtesy: Paul describes the letter he is presently composing as though it were already a finished, past event — the vantage point his readers will have once it reaches them. "The more boldly" is a true comparative, boldness justified precisely by their fullness of goodness, and "in some sort" limits that boldness to certain plain passages rather than the whole letter.

For "minister" Paul reaches past the ordinary word for a servant, *diakonos* (diakonos), and chooses *leitourgos* (leitourgos) — the term for a public officer, and in sacred contexts, a temple priest. The companion verb *leitourgeō* (leitourgeo) is the word used of priests and Levites at their sacred duties. Paul casts his gospel preaching as a priestly service, with the believing Gentiles themselves as the offering he presents, made acceptable through the Spirit's sanctifying work.
translation: But I myself stand fully persuaded concerning you, my brothers, that you yourselves also are full of goodness, having been filled to completion with all knowledge, so that you are able to keep on admonishing one another. Yet I write to you the more boldly, in some measure, as one reminding you again, because of the grace given to me from God that I should be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, serving as a priest in the good news of God, so that the offering up of the Gentiles may become acceptable, having been sanctified by the Holy Spirit.

label: Romans 15:17–21
text:
Paul's "glorying" is "in Christ Jesus" — the boast belongs entirely to what Christ accomplished through him, not to his own résumé; he immediately shuts down any claim about "anything which Christ did not work through me." The miracles he cites come under two different Greek words with different emphases: *sēmeion* (semeion), "sign," stresses the evidential force of a miracle — the credential proving the message came from God — while *teras* (teras), "wonder," stresses its startling, memorable character. Paul's ministry carried both kinds of force.

"Fully preached" translates *plēroō* (pleroo) in the perfect tense with *euaggelion* (euangelion), "good news" — Paul does not mean he reached every individual from Jerusalem to Illyricum, but that he brought the gospel's proclamation to completion across that whole territory, leaving nothing undone in his assigned task. "Strived" is *philotimeomai* (philotimeomai), literally "moved by love of honor" — his refusal to preach where Christ was already named was a matter of honor, not rivalry: he simply would not build on another man's foundation.
translation: I therefore keep my glorying in Christ Jesus, in the things pertaining to God. For I will not dare to speak of anything except what Christ has worked through me, resulting in the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed, by the power of attesting signs and astonishing wonders, by the power of the Holy Spirit — so that from Jerusalem and around as far as Illyricum I have brought the proclaiming of the good news of Christ to completion. And in this way I have made it a point of honor to keep announcing the good news, not where Christ has already been named, so that I would not be building on another man's foundation; but, just as it stands written, Those to whom no report concerning him was made, they shall see, and those who have not heard, they shall understand.

label: Romans 15:22–24
text: "Hindered" is imperfect tense — not a single roadblock but a repeated, ongoing series of hindrances, one thing after another keeping Paul from Rome. "Place" is *topos* (topos), meaning "scope, opportunity for acting" rather than a literal spot on the map — Paul means there is no more room left for his kind of pioneering work in the regions he has already covered. "Filled" is *empimplēmi* (empiplemi), "to have one's fill, to be satiated," and the qualifier "in part" deliberately softens that word — Paul admits he would gladly stay far longer than the brief visit he is proposing; only a partial satisfaction is realistic before he presses on toward Spain.
translation: For this reason I have been repeatedly hindered, by the many things, from coming to you. But now, no longer having scope for work in these regions, and having had a longing to come to you for many years now, whenever I journey to Spain, I hope, as I am passing through, to see you and to be sent on my way there by you — once I have first been in some part satisfied with your company.

label: Romans 15:25–27
text:
"It pleased" is *eudokeō* (eudokeo), used of a formal, official resolution by the churches, yet carrying the flavor of something done gladly and freely rather than under compulsion — a formal vote that was also a warm impulse. "The poor saints" is better read as "the poor of the saints" — not every believer in Jerusalem was poor; this names a subset.
