"Contribution" is *koinōnia* (koinonia), the same root behind "fellowship" elsewhere and "share" in Hebrews 13:16 — the collection is not merely a gift handed across a gap but the Gentile churches entering into common cause with the Jerusalem believers, making the need their own. Paul frames the exchange as a debt in two currencies: the Gentiles received spiritual riches from the Jews and now owe back material ones.

"Performed" (*epiteleō*, epiteleo) means to carry a task through to completion, and "sealed" (*sphragizō*, sphragizo) draws on the range of a seal's uses in the ancient world — authenticating, securing as property, finalizing. Paul pictures the delivered collection as something formally certified and closed out, the tangible "fruit" grown from the Gentiles' reception of the gospel.
translation: But now I am journeying to Jerusalem, ministering to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a certain joint contribution for the poor of the saints who are in Jerusalem. They were pleased to do it, and they are debtors to them, since the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual things, and are therefore obligated to serve them in material things. When, then, I have carried this through to completion and have sealed to them this fruit, I will go on through you into Spain — and I know that when I come to you, I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.

label: Romans 15:30–33
text: The "for" in "for our Lord Jesus Christ" and "for the love of the Spirit" is *dia* (dia) with the genitive, marking agency — "through," not "for the sake of." Paul is not just citing these as reasons; he is naming the actual means by which he expects the Romans to be moved to pray. "Strive together" is *sunagonizomai* (sunagonizomai), an athletic term for teammates competing shoulder to shoulder in the games — Paul wants the Romans wrestling alongside him in prayer with the coordinated intensity a team brings to a contest. "Believe not" is *apeitheō* (apeitheo), built from *peithō* (peitho), "to persuade," with a negating prefix — literally "those resistant to persuasion," people who have set themselves against being won over. That is the danger Paul is bracing for in Judea.
translation: Now I beg you, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love that the Spirit produces, to keep contending together with me, as teammates, in your prayers to God on my behalf, that I may be rescued from those resistant to persuasion in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may prove acceptable to the saints, so that I may come to you in joy by the will of God and find rest together with you. Now may the God of peace be with you all. Amen.

label: Romans 16:5
text: "The church in their house" reflects the reality of first-century Christian gathering — there were no dedicated church buildings for centuries, so congregations met wherever a well-off believer could open a home. Calling Epaenetus the "firstfruits of Asia" locates him among the very first converts in the Roman province of Asia (the western part of what is now Turkey) — a title of honor marking him as an early harvest, the first sign of a larger ingathering still to come.
translation: Also greet the assembly that meets in their house. Greet Epaenetus, my beloved, who is the firstfruits of Asia to Christ.

label: Romans 16:6–9
text: The description of Mary's labor uses a verb for wearisome effort pushed to the point of exhaustion — not polite praise but a specific claim about strenuous, costly work on the Romans' behalf. "Kinsmen" (*suggenēs*, syngenes) most likely marks Andronicus and Junia as Paul's fellow Jews rather than literal blood relatives — it would be striking if this many people in a Roman congregation were all his actual family. "Fellowprisoners" (*sunaichmalōtos*, synaichmalotos) is a military term for a fellow captive taken in war, suggesting they shared one of Paul's imprisonments outright. And "were in Christ before me" uses the perfect tense of "to become" — not simply "they became believers earlier" but "they came to be in Christ, and remain so" — the same tense Paul reaches for elsewhere to underline the permanence of a believer's standing.
translation: Greet Mary, who has labored, and keeps having labored, to the point of exhaustion for you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my fellow-countrymen and my fellow-prisoners, who are men of note among the apostles, who also have come to be in Christ, and remain so, before me. Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow-worker in Christ, and Stachys, my beloved.

label: Romans 16:10–16
text: Apelles is called "approved in Christ" with a verb that pictures him as already tested and found genuine — not a hope but a verdict already rendered. The greetings to "those of the household of Aristobulus" and "of Narcissus" point to slaves: household servants commonly kept a former master's name even after being sold or inherited by someone else, so these are greetings to believers within slave households, a quiet witness to how far the gospel had already reached down the social ladder. The "holy kiss" takes an ordinary Near Eastern greeting custom and marks it off with a single word — *holy* — as something now belonging distinctly to the family of God rather than mere social courtesy.
translation: Greet Apelles, the one who has been tested and found genuine in Christ. Greet those who belong to the household of Aristobulus. Greet Herodion, my fellow-countryman. Greet those who belong to the household of Narcissus, who are in the Lord. Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, women who keep laboring to the point of exhaustion in the Lord. Greet Persis the beloved, who labored hard in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who is also mine. Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers with them. Greet Philologus, and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints with them. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.

label: Romans 16:17–20
text:
"Mark" is *skopeō* (skopeo), a continuous "keep your eye fixed on" rather than a single glance — Paul wants ongoing vigilance, not a one-time warning heeded and forgotten. "Avoid" is then *ekklinō* (ekklino), built on the idea of leaning away — deliberately angling yourself out of someone's path. The false teachers, Paul says, serve "their own belly" (*koilia*, koilia, the whole stomach cavity) — a blunt image for self-interest generally, set against genuine service to Christ. Their method is *chrēstologia* (chrestologia), smooth talk imitating goodness, and *eulogia* (eulogia, the root of our word "eulogy"), polished language dressed up to sound fine.

Two different Greek words lie behind "simple" here. In verse 18 it is *akakos* (akakos), literally "not evil" — a neutral, undefended innocence, naivety rather than virtue, precisely the quality that leaves someone vulnerable. In verse 19 it is *akeraios* (akeraios), "unmixed, without foreign admixture" — a positive purity, moral integrity untouched by corrupting influence, which is what Paul actually wants for the Romans: wisdom paired with an unmixed resistance to evil rather than mere naivety. "Bruise" (*suntribō*, syntribo) is a violent verb, "crush, trample underfoot" — an echo of the ancient promise that the woman's seed would crush the serpent's head.
translation: Now I beg you, brothers, keep a constant watch on those who are producing the divisions and the snares that run contrary to the teaching you learned, and keep leaning away from them. For such people are not serving as slaves to our Lord Christ but to their own bellies, and by their smooth talk that imitates goodness, and their polished fine language, they keep deceiving the hearts of the unguarded. Your obedience has reached the ears of everyone; over you, then, I keep rejoicing. But I want you to be wise regarding what is good, and pure, unmixed with evil, regarding what is evil. And the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus be with you.

label: Romans 16:21–24
text: Timothy's name is built from *timaō* (timao), "to honor," and *theos* (theos), "God" — "one who honors God," a name given in hope a child would grow to embody it. Tertius, who pens his own greeting rather than relaying Paul's words, was the secretary taking dictation for the letter — a practical necessity, since Paul's eyesight had been damaged by illness. "Wrote" here, like Paul's own "have written" earlier in the letter, is an epistolary aorist: Tertius describes his own act of writing from the standpoint of the Roman readers, who will encounter it as something already done, even though for Tertius it is happening in the moment. "Chamberlain" translates *oikonomos* (oikonomos), "manager, steward" — a term used broadly for someone overseeing property or public affairs, here marking Erastus's civic post managing the city's business.
translation: Timothy my fellow-worker greets you, and so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my fellow-countrymen. I, Tertius, who am writing this letter, greet you in the Lord. Gaius, host to me and to the whole assembly, greets you. Erastus, the city's steward, greets you, and Quartus the brother.

label: Romans 16:25–27
text:
"Stablish" is *stērizō* (sterizo), "to make firm, set fast" — the same wish Paul voiced at the letter's opening (1:11), where he longed to impart some gift that would establish the Romans; now, at the close, he hands that task entirely to God, since only God can actually secure it. Paul calls it "my gospel" not because he invented it but because it carries his own stamp — the message as he received it directly and characteristically emphasized it: salvation entirely by faith, free and offered without distinction.

"Mystery" is *mustērion* (mysterion), something once hidden and unknowable that has now been disclosed and can be understood — not a puzzle still unsolved but a secret now opened. It was "kept in silence" (a passive verb, *sigaō*, sigao) through the ages before creation and has now been "made manifest" (*phaneroō*, phaneroo, "to make visible") through the prophetic writings, by God's own command. "Everlasting" is better read as "eternal" — *aiōnios* (aionios) means without beginning as well as without end, a stronger claim than "everlasting," which could technically have a starting point.
translation: Now to him who is able to establish you according to my gospel, even the proclamation of Jesus Christ, according to the uncovering of the mystery that has been kept in silence through times eternal, but now has been made visible, and through prophetic writings, according to the command of the eternal God, has been made known for the obedience of faith among all nations — to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, be the glory forever. Amen.
